anomalies.what: No project has a geometry at all - the PostGIS MultiPolygon column is 100% NULL.
anomalies.evidence: kubectl ... -tAc "SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE \"projectGeographicLocation\" IS NOT NULL), count(*) FILTER (WHERE \"projectGeographicLocation\" IS NULL) FROM projects_project;" -> 0|43. Re-checked raw: SELECT count(*) FROM projects_project WHERE "projectGeographicLocation" IS NOT NULL -> 0. The SQL dump agrees: the projectGeographicLocation position in COPY public.projects_project is \N for every row. postgis_version() -> 3.3, column declared geometry(MultiPolygon,4326).
anomalies.impact: An importer written to LEFT JOIN or to require ST_AsGeoJSON output will look correct in code review and produce nothing, and nobody will notice the map endpoint is dead because it is dead in Django too. Worse, an importer that treats a missing geometry as a hard error will abort on row one. Conversely, a naive ST_AsGeoJSON(NULL) returns SQL NULL (not the string 'null'), so a column typed UnicodeText silently gets NULL - which is right, but only by accident.
anomalies.handling: Emit the extraction SQL guarded on both NULL and empty: SELECT id, ST_AsGeoJSON(ST_Transform("projectGeographicLocation", 4326), 7) FROM projects_project WHERE "projectGeographicLocation" IS NOT NULL AND NOT ST_IsEmpty("projectGeographicLocation"); store the result string in c4w_project.geom_geojson and NULL otherwise. Expect 0 rows today and assert that /project/<slug>/geojson degrades to 404/empty rather than 500 for all 43 projects. Keep the query in the importer so a later Django edit is picked up on a re-run.

anomalies.what: The modeltranslation _en shadow columns are byte-identical duplicates of their base columns; the two fields that only ever existed in the shadow are empty on BOTH sides.
anomalies.evidence: For description: non-empty base=43, non-empty _en=43, equal=43, differing=0, base-empty-but-_en-set=0, _en-empty-but-base-set=0. Same shape for aim (43/43/43/0/0/0) and howToParticipate (39/39/39/0/0/0). equipment and equipment_en are both NULL in 43/43 rows (0 empty strings); citizen_science_aspects_description and _en likewise 43/43 NULL.
anomalies.impact: An importer that 'prefers the _en column and falls back to the base' and one that does the opposite produce identical output here - so the choice is untestable against production and will drift. An importer that CONCATENATES or that writes both into extras doubles every description. And a spec that assumes the _en column is where the English lives would report equipment/cs_aspects as 'lost in translation' when in fact they were never filled.
anomalies.handling: Read the BASE column (description, aim, "howToParticipate", equipment, citizen_science_aspects_description) and drop all five _en columns unconditionally. Add a pre-flight assertion to the importer: fail loudly if any row has a non-empty _en that differs from its base, so a future Django edit cannot slip English content past the drop.

anomalies.impact:
logic/sanitize.ALLOWED_TAGS is [b,i,em,strong,u,a,p,ul,ol,li,br,h3,h4,blockquote] - it does not include div, span, font, section, sub, h2 or o:p, so bleach(strip=True) removes those tags while keeping their text. That is mostly benign, but the single

and

anomalies.what: There is no slug in Django, and slugifying the 43 real names collides in 6 pairs - and the naive legacy_id-ascending assignment hands the clean slug to the UNAPPROVED twin in 4 of the 6.
anomalies.evidence: Ran ckanext.c4w.text.slugify over all 43 names: 37 distinct slugs. Collisions: 'test-project' [6,7], 'preservamos' [15,16], 'freshwater-watch-parma' [21,22], 'citizen-science-engagement-in-cauvery-delta' [25,26], 'testing-water-quality-credits-in-south-africa-s-mthinzima-catchment' [40,41], 'fountains-of-bulgaria' [43,44]. Approval per pair (SELECT id, approved, moderated, "totalAccesses"): 15=true/509 vs 16=false/11; 21=false/6 vs 22=true/500; 25=false/1 vs 26=true/350; 40=true/248 vs 41=false/0; 43=true/1894 vs 44=false/1; 6 and 7 both false. Note ids 40 and 41 differ only by a leading ': ' in the name (': Testing Water Quality Credits...'), which slugify strips.
anomalies.impact: c4w_project has a UNIQUE index on slug (ix_c4w_project_slug), so a plain slugify aborts the import on the 7th name with an IntegrityError. Using db.unique_slug in id order does not abort, but for pairs 21/22, 25/26 and 43/44 (and 40/41 depending on ordering) the live, approved, high-traffic project gets '<name>-2' while the invisible unapproved duplicate owns the canonical URL - a permanent, hard-to-reverse mistake because the module docstring says a slug is assigned once and never moved.
anomalies.handling: Assign slugs in a deterministic priority order rather than by id: ORDER BY approved DESC, moderated DESC, "totalAccesses" DESC, id ASC, calling db.unique_slug for each. That gives 15, 22, 26, 40, 43 the clean slug and their twins the -2 suffix, and the id tie-break keeps 6/7 stable across re-runs. Persist the slug against legacy_id on first import and never recompute it on a later run.

anomalies.what: Six of the 43 rows are accidental double submissions - near-identical twins that also duplicated their image uploads under different media paths.
anomalies.evidence: Per-pair jsonb diff of every scalar column. Pair 43/44 differs only in id, dateCreated/dateUpdated, firstAccess, totalAccesses, approved, moderated, a truncated achievements string, and the three image paths (e.g. image1 'images/2026-04-03_131304044646_944_Fountains_website_(Facebook_Cover).png' vs '...044949_121_Fountains_website_(Facebook_Cover).png' - same filename, different upload timestamp). Pair 40/41 is worse: the approved twin 40 has author/author_email/mainOrganisation_id set but EMPTY number_of_participants and duration_of_involvement, while the unapproved twin 41 has '50 ' and '1 month ' and no author. Pairs 21/22 and 25/26 both have mainOrganisation_id NULL on one side and set on the other. Across all rows: 91 non-empty image paths, all 91 distinct as strings.
anomalies.impact: Naively importing all 43 uploads 91 files where ~12 are byte-identical re-uploads of the same picture, doubling media storage and producing two c4w_media_map rows for one image. It also publishes 9 unapproved shadow rows that a sysadmin will see in the moderation queue as duplicates, and it means the approved project 40 permanently lacks the participant-count data its twin holds.
anomalies.handling: Import all 43 rows (legacy_id is the idempotency key and a dropped row breaks the /project/<int> redirect), but key c4w_media_map by sha256 as well as legacy_path so an identical file uploads once and both rows point at the same URL. Surface the six twin pairs in the import report as a manual merge/hide list rather than merging them automatically - the 40/41 case shows the field-level winner is not always the approved row.

anomalies.what: lead_partner_type uses the EMPTY STRING, never NULL, for 'not answered'.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE lead_partner_type IS NULL), count(*) FILTER (WHERE lead_partner_type=''), count(*) FILTER (WHERE lead_partner_type<>'') FROM projects_project -> 0 | 12 | 31. Grouped: ''=12, academic=16, ngo=5, government=4, private=3, citizen=2, other=1. The same '' convention holds for every C4W free-text column (achievements NULL=0/empty=22, challenges NULL=0/empty=29, target_group NULL=0/empty=14, ai_description NULL=0/empty=38, ...) and for url (8), projectlocality (11), author (12), author_email (11), image1 (5), image2 (14), image3 (19).
anomalies.impact: '' is not a member of constants.LEAD_PARTNER_TYPES, so a validator that checks membership rejects 12 of 43 projects and the whole import fails; one that does not check writes '' into extras, and constants.label_for('lead_partner_type','') returns '' - the project page then renders a 'Lead partner type:' label with nothing after it. The same class of bug turns 19 blank image3 fields into 19 attempted uploads of the file at MEDIA_ROOT + '' (the media root directory itself).
anomalies.handling: Normalise every empty string to None at the top of the row mapper, before any per-field logic, and only then validate closed vocabularies. Treat '' and NULL as the same absent value everywhere in this table - the choice between them in Django is an artefact of blank=True vs null=True, not a distinction the data intends.

anomalies.what: Deriving the training_level term by slugifying the lookup label produces terms that are NOT in the vocabulary, for 33 of the 35 projects that have one.
anomalies.evidence: projects_traininglevel rows are 1='No prerequisite knowledge', 2='Brief training needed', 3='Extensive training needed', 4='Other'. normalise_term of those gives 'no-prerequisite-knowledge', 'brief-training-needed', 'extensive-training-needed', 'other', but constants.TRAINING_LEVELS terms are 'no-prerequisite', 'brief-training', 'extensive-training', 'other' - three of four do not match (verified by running text.normalise_term against dict(constants.TRAINING_LEVELS)). Usage: training_level_id 1 -> 13 projects, 2 -> 19, 3 -> 1, 4 -> 2, NULL -> 8. So 33 rows get an invalid term. The mirror-image trap exists on status: normalise_term('Not yet started') = 'not-yet-started', which is not in constants.STATUSES (the term is 'not-started'), affecting the 5 projects with status_id=1; slugifying projects_status.status_code instead gives 'not-started' and all six codes land exactly on the vocabulary.
anomalies.impact: A single generic 'slugify the label' helper applied to all three single-valued lookups is the obvious implementation and it silently corrupts two of them. The values still store and still render (constants.label_for falls back to the term itself), so nothing raises - the failure shows up later as a Status facet that never matches 'Not yet started' and a training-level display reading 'no-prerequisite-knowledge'. difficultyLevel is the one that DOES survive a naive slugify ('Not Indicated'/'Easy'/'Medium'/'Hard' -> not-indicated/easy/medium/hard, all four valid), which is exactly what makes the bug look tested.
anomalies.handling: Use per-lookup mappings, not one helper. status: text.normalise_term(projects_status.status_code) (or an exact-label lookup of projects_status.status against constants.STATUSES - both agree on all six). training_level: exact-label lookup {label: term for term, label in constants.TRAINING_LEVELS}[projects_traininglevel.name]. difficultyLevel: normalise_term is safe. In all three cases assert the resulting term is in the vocabulary and fail the row loudly rather than storing an unknown slug.

anomalies.what: uses_ai and indigenous_knowledge disagree with their own description fields on 3 rows.
anomalies.evidence: uses_ai=true on ids 14, 19, 30, 47 (4 rows) but ai_description is non-empty on 5 rows - id 45 has uses_ai=false and ai_description='No AI was used'. indigenous_knowledge=true on ids 17, 27, 38 (3 rows) but indigenous_description is non-empty on 5 - id 14 has indigenous_knowledge=false with 114 characters of text, and id 47 has indigenous_knowledge=false with 1293 characters ('In Dji Mansa, we integrate local and traditional knowledge systems alongside scientific approaches...'). The converse never happens: 0 rows have the flag true and an empty description.
anomalies.impact: An importer that derives the boolean from the description (`uses_ai = bool(ai_description)`) flips id 45 to true and asserts a project uses AI when its own text says it does not. An importer that gates the description on the flag (`if uses_ai: store ai_description`) discards 1293 characters of substantive indigenous-knowledge content from project 47 - the longest such text in the corpus - and the loss is invisible because the flag renders as 'No'.
anomalies.handling: Import both independently and verbatim: the boolean from the boolean column, the text from the text column. Do not derive one from the other in either direction. If the project page hides the description behind the flag, change the template to render the description whenever it is non-empty; flag these 3 rows in the import report for an editor to reconcile.

anomalies.what: start_date and end_date are timestamptz at exactly midnight UTC, and casting them to a Date under a non-UTC session shifts every one back a day.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT DISTINCT to_char(start_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC','HH24:MI:SS') -> single row '00:00:00' (same for end_date). Demonstrated: SET TIME ZONE 'America/Santiago'; SELECT id, start_date, start_date::date, (start_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date FROM projects_project WHERE id IN (8,12,13) -> id 8: '2015-12-31 21:00:00-03' | 2015-12-31 | 2016-01-01; id 12: 2016-09-30 vs 2016-10-01; id 13: 2025-03-14 vs 2025-03-15. Under SET TIME ZONE 'UTC' the bare ::date gives the correct 2016-01-01 / 2016-10-01 / 2025-03-15.
anomalies.impact: Every one of the 30 start dates and 19 end dates lands on the wrong day whenever the importer's DB session or Python locale is west of UTC - and the shift is one day, so it looks plausible and no test catches it. The same cast applies to dateCreated/dateUpdated going into c4w_project.created/modified, which are TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE: handing psycopg a tz-aware datetime lets Postgres resolve the offset against the session TimeZone, so the default listing order can be silently skewed by hours.
anomalies.handling: Convert explicitly in the extraction query, never by implicit cast: (start_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date, (end_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date, ("dateCreated" AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') and ("dateUpdated" AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'). In Python, call .astimezone(datetime.timezone.utc).replace(tzinfo=None) before binding to the naive DateTime columns, and set the importer's session to UTC as a belt-and-braces guard.

anomalies.what: Two Django creators have usernames that CKAN cannot hold, and created_by must carry the CKAN user UUID rather than the username.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT u.id, u.name, count(p.id), string_agg(p.id::text) FROM authtools_user u JOIN projects_project p ON p.creator_id=u.id WHERE u.name !~ '^[a-z0-9_-]{2,}$' GROUP BY 1,2 -> (1,'Admin',2,'6,7') and (5,'Karen',2,'24,11'). CKAN's user name validator accepts only [a-z0-9_-]. Across all 62 users the illegal names are Admin, Jorge, Karen, Jef, Jef, Liza - and ids 10 and 17 are BOTH 'Jef', so lower('jef') is not even unique (SELECT lower(name), count(*) FROM authtools_user GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>1 -> jef|2). 31 distinct creators overall, 0 dangling creator_id, all 31 accounts is_active=true. authtools_user has no 'username' column at all - 'name' is it.
anomalies.impact: Two failure modes compound. First, storing the Django username in c4w_project.created_by breaks authorship silently: logic/action/projects.py _visible_to compares project.created_by == user.id (a CKAN UUID), so every author would be denied access to their own unapproved project and only sysadmins could see the moderation queue correctly. Second, an importer that lowercases 'Admin' to 'admin' to make it CKAN-legal will happily attach 2 projects to whatever unrelated account owns 'admin' on the CKAN instance - and lowercasing 'Jef' would map two distinct Django accounts onto one CKAN user.
anomalies.handling: Resolve authtools_user.name through CKAN user_show and store the returned user.id (UUID) in created_by; on NotFound leave created_by NULL and log the (legacy_id, django_username) pair. Never create a CKAN user, never case-fold or otherwise repair a username to force a match. The four affected projects (6, 7, 11, 24) are precisely the four throwaway test rows, so a NULL there costs nothing.

anomalies.what: Four of the 43 'projects' are throwaway test rows, and their content is a single word.
anomalies.evidence:
SELECT id, name, approved, "totalAccesses", creator_id: 6='Test project' approved=false accesses=0 creator=1(Admin); 7='Test project' approved=false accesses=1 creator=1; 11='Test' approved=false accesses=3 creator=5(Karen); 24='Test 5/2' approved=false accesses=1 creator=5. Their descriptions are '

This is a test

', '

Test

', '

Test description

'; all have empty images, empty url, empty author, no mainOrganisation, no dates.
anomalies.impact: They are all approved=false so the public listing (query._public_filter: approved IS TRUE AND hidden IS NOT TRUE -> 34 rows) never shows them, but they do occupy 4 of the 43 legacy_ids, they claim the slugs 'test-project', 'test-project-2', 'test' and 'test-5-2', and they will appear in the sysadmin moderation queue forever as pending items nobody will ever action.
anomalies.handling: Import them so legacy_id coverage stays complete and the /project/<int> redirect never 404s, but flag them in the import report as candidates for hidden=True. Do not decide this in the mapper - it is an editorial call. Verify after import that the public listing returns exactly 34 rows.

anomalies.what: Eight scalar columns are 100% NULL and one boolean pair is 100% false, so a spec derived from the Django model would map nine fields that carry no data.
anomalies.evidence: Nullability census over 43 rows: country NULL=43, host NULL=43, origin NULL=43, "originURL" NULL=43, "originUID" NULL=43, "originDatabase_id" NULL=43 (and SELECT count(*) FROM projects_origindatabase -> 0), equipment NULL=43, equipment_en NULL=43, citizen_science_aspects_description NULL=43. "doingAtHome" false=43/true=0, "participatingInaContest" false=43/true=0, featured false=43/true=0.
anomalies.impact: Mapping the origin/* block and originDatabase_id creates a c4w vocabulary with zero terms and a FK resolver that can never resolve, which is dead code that later readers will assume is load-bearing. Mapping country (the single-value legacy CountryField) alongside the projects_project_projectCountry M2M invites a second, always-empty country facet that competes with the real one. And featured=0 means the 'Featured' ordering in constants.PROJECT_ORDERINGS and any featured strip on the homepage render empty on day one - which will read as a bug in the new site rather than as faithful migration.
anomalies.handling: Drop country, host, origin, originURL, originUID, originDatabase_id, doingAtHome and participatingInaContest with the reason recorded in the mapping table. Keep equipment and cs_aspects mapped (they are live form fields in constants.PROJECT_FORM_STEPS) but expect them absent from every row. Import featured verbatim and tell the site owner up front that no project is featured, so somebody chooses one deliberately instead of filing a bug.

anomalies.what: Free-text values carry stray leading/trailing whitespace, and in three cases the wrong kind of value entirely.
anomalies.evidence: Rows where the value differs from btrim(value): name=1 (id 39), url=3 (ids 21, 22, 31), author=5 (ids 21, 22, 27, 29, 40), author_email=3 (ids 21, 22, 40), projectlocality=4, "fundingProgram"=2 (ids 27, 47); description=0, aim=0. The trailing space is the ONLY reason those 3 emails fail ^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$. Separately, ids 21 and 22 have author='https://www.parmasostenibile.it/#freshwaterwatch  ' (a URL in the contact-name field) and id 38 has author='Info@homeriverbioblitz.org' (an email in the name field).
anomalies.impact: Untrimmed values break exact-match lookups and dedup checks, and an email validator applied at import time rejects 3 otherwise-fine projects purely on a trailing byte. The untrimmed name on id 39 does not change its slug (slugify strips) but does render with a visible gap. The author-field misuse means a 'mailto:' or 'name' render on three project pages shows a raw URL or a duplicated email address.
anomalies.handling: btrim every character/text column in the mapper before any validation or emptiness test. Do not attempt to repair the three misused author values automatically - carry them verbatim and list them in the import report; guessing a person's name from a URL is not the importer's job.

anomalies.what: Two rows have dateUpdated strictly earlier than dateCreated, and the media filenames the importer must fetch include uppercase extensions and non-ASCII characters.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT id, "dateCreated", "dateUpdated" FROM projects_project WHERE "dateUpdated" < "dateCreated" -> id 33: created 2026-02-10 16:14:44.266306+00 vs updated 2026-02-10 16:14:44+00; id 38: created 2026-02-11 11:28:14.845563+00 vs updated 2026-02-11 11:28:14+00 - in both cases the update timestamp lost its sub-second component. Media: extension histogram over the 91 non-empty image paths is png=44, PNG=2, jpg=25, JPG=5, jpeg=11, JPEG=4 (11 uppercase); 2 paths contain non-ASCII ('images/2025-11-13_151511110505_879_Sin_título.png' and its twin), 2 contain a comma, 10 contain parentheses, 2 contain a tilde ('PRE504~1.PNG'); max path length 156 of the 300 allowed; all 91 start with 'images/'.
anomalies.impact: An importer that asserts modified >= created aborts on two rows. An importer that lowercases or regex-matches '\.(png|jpg|jpeg)$' case-sensitively skips 11 real images, leaving 11 project cards without artwork. A media fetcher that builds a URL by naive string concatenation without percent-encoding will 404 on the accented, comma-bearing and parenthesised filenames - and because the same picture also exists under the duplicate twin's path, the failure looks intermittent.
anomalies.handling: Do not assert an ordering between created and modified; clamp modified = max(modified, created) only if the listing sort needs monotonicity, and record the two rows. For media, match extensions case-insensitively, percent-encode each path segment when constructing the source URL, and normalise the stored legacy_path in c4w_media_map to the exact byte string from the database (not a normalised or lowercased form) so the /citizens4water/media/<path> redirect keeps matching inbound links.

open_questions: constants.COLUMN_VOCABULARIES documents training_level and lead_partner_type as 'Single-valued closed fields stored as native columns, not as term links', but c4w_project_table in db.py has neither a training_level nor a lead_partner_type column. I have mapped both to extras (keys 'training_level' and 'lead_partner_type', matching their names in constants.PROJECT_FORM_STEPS steps 3 and 6). Confirm that is intended, or add the two columns - 35 of 43 projects have a training level and 31 have a lead partner type, so if either is ever faceted it needs a column and an index.

c4w_project has no column and no obvious extras home for the fact that a project was never given a geometry. Since 43/43 are NULL, should geom_geojson be dropped from the table for v1, or kept as the forward-compatible slot it currently is? I have assumed kept.

Six twin pairs (6/7, 15/16, 21/22, 25/26, 40/41, 43/44) are accidental double submissions. Import all 43 and let a moderator hide the duplicates, or have the importer hide the non-approved twin automatically? Pair 40/41 complicates a pure 'keep the approved one' rule: the unapproved twin 41 holds number_of_participants='50 ' and duration_of_involvement='1 month ' that the approved twin 40 lacks.

The four test projects (legacy ids 6, 7, 11, 24) are all unapproved. Import as-is, import with hidden=True, or skip? Skipping breaks /project/6 and /project/11 redirects, which is why I default to importing them.

Two project creators ('Admin' id 1 and 'Karen' id 5, covering projects 6, 7, 11, 24) have names CKAN cannot use as usernames, so created_by will be NULL for those four rows. Confirm NULL is acceptable rather than falling back to a designated migration account.

Should the three no-scheme urls (ids 15, 16, 38: 'www.preservamos.ar', 'www.homeriverbioblitz.org') be rewritten with an https:// prefix at import time, or stored verbatim and fixed in the template's link builder? I have specified the import-time prefix.

howToParticipate and equipment are live project-form fields but have no native column. Confirm the extras keys should be 'how_to_participate' and 'equipment' (as named in constants.PROJECT_FORM_STEPS) rather than the Django camelCase names.
featured is false on all 43 rows, so the 'Featured' ordering and any homepage featured strip are empty after import. Does someone need to pick featured projects as part of the cutover?

verdict.area: Project: native columns of projects_project (scalars + single-valued FKs)

corrections.field: row_counts — "projects_project=43 (min id=6, max id=49, 6 ids missing in range)"
corrections.problem: The gap count is wrong by a factor of six. The id span 6..49 is 44 values and there are 43 rows, so exactly ONE id is missing, not six. The missing id is 10.
corrections.fix: Restate as: projects_project=43, min id=6, max id=49, exactly 1 missing id (10). Any /project/<int> redirect smoke test should assert 43 live legacy ids and exactly one 404 (id 10), not six.
corrections.evidence: kubectl --context=default -n ckan exec c4w-postgres-0 -- psql -U citizens4water -d c4w_import -tAc "SELECT count(*), min(id), max(id) FROM projects_project;" -> 43|6|49. And: "SELECT count(*)||' rows, id span '||(max(id)-min(id)+1) FROM projects_project;" -> '43 rows, id span 44'. And: "SELECT string_agg(g::text,',') FROM generate_series(6,49) g WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM projects_project p WHERE p.id=g);" -> 10

corrections.problem: The spec lists projects_status and projects_difficultylevel in tables_covered but never enumerates their columns, so it silently omits their two modeltranslation shadow columns. It gave every _en column on projects_project an explicit DROP row with a reason; the lookup tables get none. A reader implementing from this spec has no instruction for them, and the 'read the _en column, it is where English lives' misreading the spec warns about elsewhere is left live here.
corrections.fix: Add explicit DROP rows: projects_status.status_en (populated, identical to status in all 6 rows) and projects_difficultylevel."difficultyLevel_en" (populated, identical to "difficultyLevel" in all 4 rows). Also add projects_origindatabase.originDatabase -> DROP (table has 0 rows). Note that projects_traininglevel has NO shadow column at all, which is why the training-level label lives only in .name.
corrections.evidence: "SELECT table_name||' :: '||column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name IN ('projects_status','projects_difficultylevel','projects_traininglevel','projects_origindatabase') ORDER BY table_name, ordinal_position;" -> projects_difficultylevel::id, ::difficultyLevel, ::difficultyLevel_en; projects_origindatabase::id, ::originDatabase; projects_status::id, ::status, ::status_en, ::status_code; projects_traininglevel::id, ::name. Values: "SELECT id||'|'||status||'|'||status_code||'|'||coalesce(status_en,'<NULL>') FROM projects_status ORDER BY id;" -> 1|Not yet started|not_started|Not yet started ... 6|Abandoned|abandoned|Abandoned (base == _en in all 6); "SELECT id||'|'||\"difficultyLevel\"||'|'||coalesce(\"difficultyLevel_en\",'<NULL>') FROM projects_difficultylevel ORDER BY id;" -> 1|Not Indicated|Not Indicated ... 4|Hard|Hard

corrections.problem: Cites a CKAN action that does not exist: 'project_access_increment in logic/action/projects.py keeps incrementing it'. There is no such symbol anywhere in the extension. The action that increments the counter is c4w_project_record_view.
corrections.fix: Rewrite as: 'Live counter — c4w_project_record_view (logic/action/projects.py:201, project.total_accesses = (project.total_accesses or 0) + 1) keeps incrementing it, and it backs the accesses ordering.' The mapping itself (int, verbatim) is correct.
corrections.evidence: grep -rn "access_increment\|total_accesses" /home/pabrojast/Proyectos/ckan-c4w/ckanext/c4w/ --include=*.py -> no hit for access_increment anywhere; logic/action/projects.py:201 'project.total_accesses = (project.total_accesses or 0) + 1' inside c4w_project_record_view, registered in get_actions() as 'c4w_project_record_view'.

corrections.problem: Justifies NULL -> False with 'the column carries default=False'. The Django column carries NO default: hidden = models.BooleanField(null=True, blank=True). Only the c4w target column has default=False. The rationale is misattributed to the source, which matters because it is the stated reason for overwriting 42 NULLs.
corrections.fix: Keep the mapping (NULL -> False; it matches c4w_project.hidden default=False and _public_filter's hidden.isnot(True)), but restate the reason as a property of the TARGET column, not the Django one. The Django tri-state is 'never touched by a moderator' for 42 rows and 'explicitly un-hidden' for exactly one (id 8) — collapsing both to False is a deliberate loss of that distinction and should be stated as such.
corrections.evidence: /home/pabrojast/Proyectos/citizens4water_platform-1/src/projects/models.py:304 -> 'hidden = models.BooleanField(null=True, blank=True)' (no default=). db.py:148 -> Column('hidden', types.Boolean, default=False). Data: "SELECT 'hidden null='||count(*) FILTER (WHERE hidden IS NULL)||' t='||count(*) FILTER (WHERE hidden)||' f='||count(*) FILTER (WHERE hidden IS FALSE) FROM projects_project;" -> hidden null=42 t=0 f=1; "SELECT string_agg(id::text,',') FROM projects_project WHERE hidden IS FALSE;" -> 8

corrections.field: anomaly 'Free-text values carry stray leading/trailing whitespace' (the census in its evidence block)
corrections.problem: The whitespace census is presented as the full list (name=1, url=3, author=5, author_email=3, projectlocality=4, fundingProgram=2, description=0, aim=0) but it stops at the identity/contact block. Eight more columns carry untrimmed values, all of them C4W free-text fields going into extras. Anyone sizing the risk from this evidence will conclude the problem is confined to six columns.
corrections.fix: Extend the census to the whole table. Additional untrimmed columns: achievements=2, target_group=2, water_parameters=3, outreach_methods=1, number_of_participants=2, duration_of_involvement=2, data_quality_initiatives=1, ai_description=1. The prescribed handling ('btrim every character/text column in the mapper') already covers them, so only the evidence needs correcting — but the understatement matters because number_of_participants and duration_of_involvement are the two the spec elsewhere holds up as the fields the unapproved twin 41 uniquely holds ('50 ' and '1 month '), i.e. the trailing space is load-bearing in its own merge argument.
corrections.evidence: Per-column: "SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE \"<col>\" <> btrim(\"<col>\")) FROM projects_project;" run over all 39 character/text columns -> achievements=2, target_group=2, water_parameters=3, outreach_methods=1, number_of_participants=2, duration_of_involvement=2, data_quality_initiatives=1, ai_description=1 (in addition to the six the spec names). Confirming the spec's own six: name=1, url=3 (ids 21,22,31), author=5, author_email=3, projectlocality=4, fundingProgram=2, description=0, aim=0.

missed_anomalies.what: Two project-scoped tables, projects_approvedprojects (34 rows) and projects_unapprovedprojects (1 row), hold a denormalised copy of the approval state — and the unapproved queue is STALE. It contains project 33, which has approved=true and also sits in projects_approvedprojects. The spec never mentions either table.
missed_anomalies.evidence: "SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='public' AND table_name LIKE 'projects%';" lists projects_approvedprojects and projects_unapprovedprojects. "SELECT count(*) FROM projects_approvedprojects;" -> 34; "SELECT count(*) FROM projects_unapprovedprojects;" -> 1; "SELECT * FROM projects_unapprovedprojects;" -> 3|33. Cross-check against the boolean: "SELECT string_agg(p.id::text,',') FROM projects_project p JOIN projects_approvedprojects a ON a.project_id=p.id WHERE p.approved IS NOT TRUE;" -> (empty) and "SELECT string_agg(p.id::text,',') FROM projects_project p WHERE p.approved IS TRUE AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM projects_approvedprojects a WHERE a.project_id=p.id);" -> (empty), so approvedprojects agrees with the boolean exactly. But "SELECT 'apr='||(SELECT count(*) FROM projects_approvedprojects WHERE project_id=33)||' unapr='||(SELECT count(*) FROM projects_unapprovedprojects WHERE project_id=33)||' project33_approved='||(SELECT approved::text FROM projects_project WHERE id=33);" -> apr=1 unapr=1 project33_approved=true. Django source: src/projects/models.py:436 class ApprovedProjects(OneToOneField(Project)) and :446 class UnApprovedProjects(OneToOneField(Project)) — real tables, not proxy models. The 9 unapproved projects are 6,7,11,16,21,24,25,41,44, none of which is in projects_unapprovedprojects.
missed_anomalies.impact: These two tables are the obvious 'moderation queue' an implementer would reach for when building the sysadmin queue the spec repeatedly promises ('they will appear in the sysadmin moderation queue forever'). Trusting them yields 34 approved + 1 unapproved = 35 of 43 projects classified and 8 in limbo, and it marks project 33 (IslandWatch, approved, public, 271 accesses) as pending review forever while simultaneously listing it as approved. Because the spec assigns them nowhere, a later reader has no signal that they were considered and rejected rather than overlooked — which is exactly the failure mode the DROP-with-a-reason rule exists to prevent.
missed_anomalies.handling: Add both to the mapping table as explicit DROPs: 'projects_approvedprojects — denormalised duplicate of projects_project.approved, verified byte-for-byte equivalent (0 disagreements in both directions), no independent information'; 'projects_unapprovedprojects — same intent but STALE: its single row (project 33) contradicts projects_project.approved=true, so it is actively wrong and must never be read'. projects_project.approved remains the sole source of truth for c4w_project.approved. If a moderation queue is built, derive it from approved/moderated, and assert at import time that projects_approvedprojects still matches the boolean so a future divergence is caught rather than inherited.

missed_anomalies.what: description and aim are the two columns the public listing free-text searches with a raw ILIKE, and the spec stores sanitised HTML into them. Six rows have a phrase split by a tag that SURVIVES the allowlist, and three rows match a search for 'http' on markup their visible text does not contain.
missed_anomalies.evidence: logic/action/projects.py:30 -> search_columns=('name', 'description', 'aim'); logic/query.py _apply_search builds pattern = u'%%%s%%' % text.strip() and getattr(model_cls, name).ilike(pattern) — a substring match straight against the stored column. Surviving-tag phrase splits (a,b,i,em,strong,u are all in sanitize.ALLOWED_TAGS): "SELECT string_agg(id::text,',' ORDER BY id) FROM projects_project WHERE (coalesce(description,'')||coalesce(aim,'')) ~ '[[:alnum:]][ ]?]*)?>[ ]?[[:alnum:]]';" -> 13,18,30,36,39,49. Concrete strings: id 39 'g E. coli levels', id 13 'e ...', id 36 'Kd). Anchor false positives (ALLOWED_ATTRS keeps href): "SELECT string_agg(id::text,',') FROM projects_project WHERE (coalesce(description,'')||coalesce(aim,'')) ~* ']*href=';" -> 18,28,36,49, versus visible text: "SELECT string_agg(id::text,',') FROM projects_project WHERE regexp_replace(coalesce(description,'')||coalesce(aim,''),'<[^>]*>','','g') ILIKE '%http%';" -> 28. So 'http' returns 4 rows of which 3 (18, 36, 49) match only their markup.
missed_anomalies.impact: A visitor searching a phrase they can read verbatim on the project page gets zero results on 6 of 43 projects — 'E. coli levels' misses project 39 because the stored text is 'E. coli levels'. Conversely the search box behaves as a markup grep: 'http', 'href', 'rel', 'nofollow' and 'target' all return hits driven by attributes nobody typed. This is not caught by any of the spec's anomalies because each field mapping is verified in isolation; the defect only appears at the junction of 'description is a native column' and 'native column X is ILIKE-searched'. It is also permanent: sanitisation happens before storage, so there is no clean text anywhere in the target schema to fall back on.
missed_anomalies.handling: Keep the sanitised HTML in description/aim for rendering, and have the mapper additionally emit a tag-stripped, entity-decoded, whitespace-collapsed plain-text shadow for each — either as extras keys ('description_text', 'aim_text') or, if search is meant to be indexed, as a real column so _apply_search can point at it. Whichever is chosen, the choice belongs in this spec, because the importer is the only thing that can produce the plain text and it cannot be recovered later from HTML that has already been rewritten. At minimum, change search_columns to a text-bearing column and say so, rather than leaving the spec implying that description/aim are searchable as written.

missed_anomalies.what: <sub> occurs in the corpus and is NOT in sanitize.ALLOWED_TAGS, so it is unwrapped at import time and the subscript is lost permanently. The spec's own evidence counts sub=10 occurrences but its handling paragraph prescribes fixes only for div/span/font/section/h2/o:p and says nothing about sub.
missed_anomalies.evidence: sanitize.py ALLOWED_TAGS = ['b','i','em','strong','u','a','p','ul','ol','li','br','h3','h4','blockquote'] — no 'sub', no 'sup'. RICH_ALLOWED_TAGS (blog bodies only) DOES include 'sub', so the wider list already concedes the need. Data: "SELECT string_agg(id::text,',' ORDER BY id) FROM projects_project WHERE (coalesce(description,'')||coalesce(aim,'')||coalesce(\"howToParticipate\",'')) ~* '<sub[ >]';" -> 36. Context: "SELECT substring(...) FROM projects_project WHERE id=36" -> 'K<sub>d</sub>), a key indicator of underwater light availability'. The distinct-tag census over description||aim||howToParticipate is a,b,br,div,em,font,h2,i,li,ol,o:p,p,section,span,strong,sub,ul.
missed_anomalies.impact: bleach.clean(..., strip=True) removes <sub> and keeps its text, so 'K<sub>d</sub>' becomes the flat string 'Kd'. For project 36 (KdUINO, an optical-oceanography project) Kd is the diffuse attenuation coefficient — the subscript is the notation, not decoration, and flattening it makes the sentence read as a different symbol. Because sanitisation runs BEFORE storage, the markup is gone from the database and no template change can restore it. The spec's handling section is where an implementer looks for the tag-by-tag decisions; sub's absence there reads as 'nothing to do'.
missed_anomalies.handling: Decide explicitly, in the mapping table, one of: (a) add 'sub' and 'sup' to sanitize.ALLOWED_TAGS — they carry no attributes and no script surface, so the restrictive list loses nothing; or (b) pre-process <sub>x</sub> to the Unicode subscript characters before sanitising, for the single-character case that covers row 36. Do not leave it to bleach's default unwrap. Record project 36 in the import report either way so an editor can eyeball the result.

missed_anomalies.what: Invisible Unicode characters (U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE, U+202F NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE) are present in the rich-text columns. They survive both bleach and the regex fallback, and btrim() does not remove them, so the spec's prescribed blankness test ('strip tags, replace  , btrim, if blank store None') cannot see through them.
missed_anomalies.evidence:
"SELECT string_agg(id::text,',') FROM projects_project WHERE aim ~ U&'\\200B';" -> 34; context: "SELECT substring(aim from greatest(1,position(U&'\200B' in aim)-60) for 120) FROM projects_project WHERE id=34;" -> '... monitor temporal changes. ​
  • Assess natural variations ...'. And "SELECT string_agg(id::text,',') FROM projects_project WHERE description ~ U&'\\202F';" -> 33, same for aim -> 33. Negative controls from the same sweep: U+FFFD=0, U+00A0=0, U+FEFF=0, U+00AD=0, other C0 control chars in description/aim/howToParticipate = 0. The spec's own blankness query uses btrim(regexp_replace(...)) = '' — btrim's default character set is ASCII space only.
missed_anomalies.impact:
Today no row consists solely of an invisible, so nothing is currently mis-stored — but the spec presents its blankness helper as the general rule for 'every rich-text field', and the helper is one CKEditor paste away from returning non-blank for a paragraph a human sees as empty, reproducing exactly the '


' bug the spec correctly caught. Separately these characters reach the rendered page and the ILIKE search index: a phrase spanning the U+200B in project 34 or the U+202F in project 33 will not match a user typing it with an ordinary space, and slugify turns both into a '-' separator (verified: slugify('a​b') == 'a-b'), so an invisible in a future project name silently changes its URL.
missed_anomalies.handling: In the mapper's text normaliser, before the blankness test: delete U+200B/U+200C/U+200D/U+FEFF and map U+00A0/U+202F/U+2009 to a plain space, then strip tags, then strip. Use a Unicode-aware strip in Python (str.strip() already handles U+00A0/U+202F but not U+200B) rather than SQL btrim. Apply the same normaliser to name before slugify so a URL cannot be decided by a character nobody can see.

missed_anomalies.what: Eighteen of the 43 rows carry CRLF line endings in the twelve C4W plain-text columns. The spec characterises these fields as 'plain text with real newlines' and prescribes rendering with white-space:pre-wrap, without noting the carriage returns.
missed_anomalies.evidence: "SELECT string_agg(id::text,',' ORDER BY id) FROM projects_project WHERE coalesce(achievements,'')||coalesce(challenges,'')||coalesce(target_group,'')||coalesce(water_parameters,'')||coalesce(outreach_methods,'')||coalesce(interesting_highlights,'') ~ E'\r';" -> 14,20,21,22,23,27,28,29,31,36,37,39,42,43,44,46,47,49 (18 rows). Same sweep found 0 rows with U+FFFD and 0 with C0 controls other than CR/LF/TAB, so CR is the only stray control character in the corpus.
missed_anomalies.impact: json.dumps writes the CR into extras as a literal \r, where it is invisible in every inspection tool. Under white-space:pre-wrap a CRLF still renders as one break, so the page looks fine and nothing surfaces the problem — but any consumer that splits on '\n' (a bulleted render of achievements, a CSV export, a diff of two imports, the twin-pair merge report the spec asks for) gets a trailing \r on every line, and a re-import comparing a normalised value against a stored one reports 18 spurious changes on every run, defeating the idempotency the legacy_id key is there to provide.
missed_anomalies.handling: Normalise \r\n and lone \r to \n in the mapper for all twelve C4W free-text columns, alongside the btrim. Do it before writing extras, so the JSON is canonical and a second import produces a byte-identical blob.

missed_anomalies.what: projects_project.name is nullable in BOTH Postgres and the Django model, while c4w_project.name is NOT NULL and the slug is derived from it. The spec closes the question with 'never NULL in the data, so the NOT NULL constraint is safe', which is true of today's snapshot but leaves the importer's behaviour undefined for the re-runs the spec elsewhere insists on.
missed_anomalies.evidence: information_schema: projects_project.name | character varying | is_nullable=YES | max_length=200. Django: src/projects/models.py:227 -> 'name = models.CharField(max_length=200, null=True, blank=True)', and :385 '__str__' returns 'Unnamed Project' if not self.name — the model explicitly anticipates a nameless project. Target: db.py c4w_project Column('name', types.UnicodeText, nullable=False) and Column('slug', ..., nullable=False) with a unique index. Behaviour on NULL, verified against the real helpers: slugify(None) == '' and slugify('') == '', and db.unique_slug does base = slugify(base) or u'item', so a nameless row would claim the slug 'item' (then 'item-2', ...) and then fail the name NOT NULL constraint mid-transaction. Current data: "SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE name IS NULL), count(*) FILTER (WHERE name='') FROM projects_project;" -> 0|0.
missed_anomalies.impact: The importer is designed to be re-runnable against a live Django database (the spec's own pre-flight assertions and 'a later Django edit is picked up on a re-run' assume this). The Django form permits a nameless draft, so the first such row aborts the whole import with a bare IntegrityError on name, after unique_slug has already consumed the slug 'item' — and on the retry it consumes 'item-2'. Nothing in the spec tells the implementer what to do, so the natural reading is that no guard is needed.
missed_anomalies.handling: State the fallback explicitly in the name row: 'name = btrim(name); if empty or NULL, skip the row and record (legacy_id, reason="no name") in the import report' — skipping is safer than synthesising a name, because a synthesised name would take a permanent slug that can never be moved. Add a pre-flight count of NULL/empty names so the run fails fast with a readable message instead of a constraint error 30 rows in.
