anomalies.what: 4 of the 7 audience labels do NOT slugify to their constants.RESOURCE_AUDIENCES term. An importer that calls text.normalise_term(label) writes terms that no filter, facet or label lookup will ever match.
anomalies.evidence:
kubectl ... -tAc "SELECT id,'['||audience||']' FROM resources_audience ORDER BY id;" returned the 7 labels. Feeding them through the real functions:
  python3 -c "from ckanext.c4w.text import normalise_term; from ckanext.c4w import constants as C; ..."
  'Community Members & Citizens'    normalise_term=community-members-citizens    constant=community-members     MISMATCH
  'CS Project Leaders & Initiators' normalise_term=cs-project-leaders-initiators constant=cs-project-leaders      MISMATCH
  'CSOs & NGOs'                     normalise_term=csos-ngos                    constant=csos-ngos              ok
  'Educators'                       normalise_term=educators                    constant=educators              ok
  'Policy & Decision Makers'        normalise_term=policy-decision-makers       constant=policy-makers          MISMATCH
  'Researchers & Academics'         normalise_term=researchers-academics        constant=researchers            MISMATCH
  'ALL Audiences'                   normalise_term=all-audiences                constant=all-audiences          ok
The same script over the 20 resources_theme labels reports 'theme mismatches: 0 / 20', so themes are safe and audiences are the exception.
anomalies.impact: All 14 rows of resources_resource_audience are affected: the 3 mismatching audiences actually in use (ids 2, 5, 6) account for 6 of the 14 links, and the remaining 8 would be written with terms that are correct only by luck. Every wrong term is invisible: c4w_term_link has no FK to the vocabulary, the audience filter (_apply_term_facets against constants-derived terms) returns zero results, the audience facet counts come back empty, and h.c4w_term_label falls back to rendering the raw slug 'researchers-academics' instead of 'Researchers & Academics'. Nothing errors.
anomalies.handling: Build a label -> term dict from constants.RESOURCE_AUDIENCES and look the Django label up in it. All 7 production labels match a constants label exactly, so no fallback is needed. An unmatched label must be a hard import error, never a silent normalise_term() fallback. Store label = the Django string verbatim. The same defensive lookup is correct for 'theme' too even though it currently agrees with slugification.

anomalies.what: There are ZERO training resources, and both training-only lookup tables are empty. Confirmed.

SELECT count(*) FROM resources_educationlevel -> 0; SELECT count(*) FROM resources_learningresourcetype -> 0; SELECT count(*) FROM "resources_resource_educationLevel" -> 0; SELECT count(*) FROM "resources_resource_learningResourceType" -> 0.
anomalies.impact: Three consequences a naive importer gets wrong by omission. (1) /citizens4water/training_resources is a live but permanently empty listing after the cutover - if that is read as an import bug someone will 'fix' it by flipping flags. (2) The education_level and learning_resource_type facets that _spec(training=True) declares will render as empty facet blocks with no terms at all, because c4w_term_link gets no rows for those vocabularies. (3) resources_resource."timeRequired" and "conditionsOfAccess" are 6-of-6 NULL for the same reason - they are training-only fields - so their fact rows never render.
anomalies.handling: Import all 6 rows with is_training_resource=False and create no education_level / learning_resource_type term links. Do not suppress the /training_resources route: emptiness is faithful to production, and the module docstring in logic/action/resources.py already records that expectation. Also note that Django's own detail route path('training_resource/<int:pk>') has no c4w equivalent (blueprint.py registers item_path=None for the training surface) - harmless, because with zero training resources no such URL has ever existed.

anomalies.what: resources_resource.hidden and .own are 100% NULL - never true, never false. A naive bool() over the whole column is fine; a naive 'NULL means unknown, be safe, hide it' is catastrophic.
anomalies.evidence:
SELECT id, 'hidden='||coalesce(hidden::text,'NULL'), 'own='||coalesce(own::text,'NULL') FROM resources_resource ORDER BY id  ->  all six rows report hidden=NULL and own=NULL.
query.py::_public_filter lines 75-76: `if hasattr(model_cls,'hidden'): query = query.filter(model_cls.hidden.isnot(True))`.
Django's resource listing never filters on hidden at all - resources/views.py:70 is `Resource.objects.filter(~Q(isTrainingResource=True))` and line 89 adds only `.filter(approved=True)`, whereas the project query on line 97 does pass hidden=False.
anomalies.impact: If NULL is mapped to True the entire resource library disappears from /citizens4water/resources with no error - hidden.isnot(True) excludes every row and the page renders an empty list. Mapping own's NULL to False instead of omitting it writes a meaningless `"own": false` into all 6 extras blobs, asserting a staff decision nobody made.
anomalies.handling: hidden: NULL -> False (or leave NULL; isnot(True) treats them identically). own: write the extras key ONLY when the source value is non-NULL, so in production the key is never written. Same rule for isTrainingResource: NULL -> False, which is also what Django's ~Q(isTrainingResource=True) does.

anomalies.what: M2M ordering is not recorded consistently, and for one resource the two candidate orderings disagree - so the imported author list can differ from what the live site prints today.
anomalies.evidence:
The join-table id order (Django's .set(self.data.getlist('authors')) insertion order, resources/forms.py:368):
  SELECT ra.id, ra.resource_id, ra.author_id, au.author FROM resources_resource_authors ra JOIN authors_author au ... ORDER BY ra.resource_id, ra.id
  resource 3 -> join ids 8,9,10 -> author ids 8,9,7 -> 'Koen Verbist; Annelies Mertens; Nilay Dogulu'
The order Postgres actually returns for the unordered query Django emits (`resource.authors.all` in resources/templates/resources/resource.html:49 has no ORDER BY):
  SELECT r.resource_id, a.id, a.author FROM authors_author a INNER JOIN resources_resource_authors r ON a.id=r.author_id WHERE r.resource_id IN (2,3,5,6)
  resource 3 -> 7 Nilay Dogulu, 8 Koen Verbist, 9 Annelies Mertens
The same unordered probe on keywords returns join-id order instead (resource 3 -> keyword ids 5, 6, 4), so the 'natural' order is plan-dependent, not a property of the data. Also SELECT id FROM resources_resource_keywords shows ids 4..13,15,16,17 - id 14 is missing, i.e. an M2M was re-set at some point.
anomalies.impact: db.terms_for orders by (vocabulary, sort_order, term). If sort_order is left at its default 0 the tie-break is the SLUG, so 'Open Hydrology' would print as annelies-mertens, koen-verbist, nilay-dogulu - alphabetical by slug, not a citation order. If sort_order is taken from the raw join id instead of a dense rank, the gap at id 14 leaves resource 7's keywords ranked 0,2,3,4, which is harmless but noisy. And for resource 3 specifically, join-id order flips the first author relative to what production renders today.
anomalies.handling: Set sort_order = dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY resource_id ORDER BY join_table.id) - 1, for all six M2M vocabularies. Join-id ASC is the defensible order because it is what .set(getlist()) recorded, i.e. the sequence the human typed in the widget; the order production happens to render is a query-plan artefact with no ORDER BY behind it. Flag resource 3 (legacy_id 3, 'Open Hydrology') for a human to confirm the citation order after the import, because that single row's authors will move.

  id 7 lic=[ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International ]  (leading AND trailing space)
  id 5 lic=[ CC BY- 4.0]   (leading space)

anomalies.handling: For every nullable text column on resources_resource - publisher, resourceDOI, license, conditionsOfAccess, imageCredit1, imageCredit2, image1, image2, url - apply `v = (v or '').strip() or None`. anomalies.what: resources_resource.creator_id 5 resolves to authtools_user.name = 'Karen', which CKAN's name_validator rejects (uppercase), so the created_by lookup can silently fail. The user table also contains a duplicate username.
anomalies.evidence:
SELECT r.id, r.creator_id, u.name FROM resources_resource r JOIN authtools_user u ON u.id=r.creator_id -> 2/5/Karen, 3/8/amertens, 4/11/anneliesduerinckx, 5/6/ckan_admin, 6/6/ckan_admin, 7/60/elibonfill.

SELECT lower(name), count(*) FROM authtools_user GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>1 -> jef|2 (ids 10 and 17, different emails).
logic/action/_common.py:68 compares `row.created_by == user.id`, so created_by must hold a CKAN user.id UUID, not a username.
anomalies.impact: If the CKAN account is stored as 'karen' an exact-name lookup on 'Karen' returns nothing and created_by is left NULL. That is silent: the row still imports and still renders publicly. The cost only shows up for unapproved or hidden rows - _common._visible_to falls through to the 'editor' relation check and denies the real author access to her own submission. For this area only resource legacy_id 2 is affected (approved, so no visible damage today), but the same resolver is shared with every other area, where 'Jef' is genuinely ambiguous between two different people.
anomalies.handling: Resolve authtools_user.name -> CKAN user via a case-insensitive lookup, and when that returns anything other than exactly one match, leave created_by NULL and log the (legacy_id, django_name) pair loudly rather than guessing. Never create the CKAN user. Report the unresolved list at the end of the run so a human can reconcile 'Karen' and the two 'Jef' accounts before the cutover.

anomalies.what: The _en modeltranslation shadow columns are byte-identical to their base columns on every row of every table in this area, so the BASE column is the one to read - but only the base column is NOT NULL.

Schema: the base columns are NOT NULL, every _en column is NULLable (dump lines 3166-3197, 3038-3043, 2988-2992, 3518-3522).
MODELTRANSLATION_LANGUAGES = ('en',) in core_code/settings/citizens4water.py:68.
anomalies.impact: The two columns are interchangeable in today's data, which means a wrong choice is invisible in testing. Reading _en is the fragile choice: it is nullable by schema, so a single row an admin later edits through a path that skips modeltranslation's sync would import as NULL into a NOT NULL-intent field (c4w_resource.name is nullable=False - the insert would fail; abstract would just go blank).
anomalies.handling: Read the BASE column everywhere - name, abstract, description_citizen_science_aspects, resources_category.text, resources_theme.theme, resources_audience.audience - and drop every *_en column. Do not COALESCE(base, _en): the base column is NOT NULL, so the coalesce never fires and only hides the decision.

open_questions: The category filter changes shape: Django filtered resources by `category__text` (resources/views.py:858, an exact match on the category NAME), while the c4w ListingSpec declares native_filters={'category': 'category_id'} and query._apply_native_filters does column.in_(values) against the UUID. Old inbound links of the form /citizens4water/resources?category=Guideline will therefore match zero rows rather than falling back to unfiltered. Should the importer/route accept a category NAME as well as a UUID for backward compatibility, or is the break acceptable?

Neither Django nor c4w expands a parent category to its children: Django matched category__text exactly, and c4w matches category_id exactly. Since 4 of the 6 resources sit on a CHILD of Text (Guideline x2, Scientific Publication x2), selecting the parent 'Text' in the two-level dependent select returns ZERO results in both systems. c4w_category.path exists precisely to make 'everything under Text' one indexed LIKE - should the resource listing start using it (path = 'Text' OR path LIKE 'Text : %'), which would be an intentional improvement over Django rather than a faithful port?

Author order for legacy_id 3 ('Open Hydrology', UNESCO 2024) is genuinely ambiguous: the join-table insertion order gives 'Koen Verbist; Annelies Mertens; Nilay Dogulu' while the live page currently renders 'Nilay Dogulu; Koen Verbist; Annelies Mertens'. I recommend join-table id ASC, but a human who knows the publication should confirm the citation order before the production run - it is the only row where the two disagree.

verdict.area: Resource library: resources_resource, the DCMI resources_category tree, the theme/audience/keyword/education-level/learning-resource-type lookups, authors_author, and every resources_resource_* join table

corrections.field: anomaly #5 (M2M ordering) — the claim that the 'natural' order is plan-dependent
corrections.problem: The spec justifies join-id ASC by asserting that the unordered probe behaves inconsistently: 'The same unordered probe on keywords returns join-id order instead (resource 3 -> keyword ids 5, 6, 4), so the natural order is plan-dependent, not a property of the data.' That is false. Both the author probe and the keyword probe return LOOKUP-TABLE id ASC, consistently, because Postgres plans both as a hash join with the lookup table as the outer seq scan. The keyword probe for resource 3 returns keyword ids 4, 5, 6 — not 5, 6, 4. The spec's central argument for its recommendation rests on a measurement that does not reproduce.
corrections.fix: Drop the 'plan-dependent' argument. State the real situation: today the live Django page renders every M2M list in lookup-table-id ASC order (a stable artefact of the hash join), and join-id ASC is a DIFFERENT order that reflects insertion sequence. Join-id ASC is still defensible as the recorded human intent, but it must be presented as a deliberate change to what the site prints, not as a tie-break between two equally arbitrary orders. Then get the author list for legacy_id 3 confirmed by a human, as the spec already recommends.
corrections.evidence:
kubectl ... -tAc "SELECT a.id||'|'||a.author FROM authors_author a INNER JOIN resources_resource_authors r ON a.id=r.author_id WHERE r.resource_id = 3;" -> 7|Nilay Dogulu / 8|Koen Verbist / 9|Annelies Mertens
kubectl ... -tAc "SELECT k.id||'|'||k.keyword FROM resources_keyword k INNER JOIN resources_resource_keywords r ON k.id=r.keyword_id WHERE r.resource_id = 3;" -> 4|citizen science / 5|Open Science / 6|Open Hydrology   (NOT 5,6,4)
Same result with the multi-row IN list: "... WHERE r.resource_id IN (2,3,5,6);" -> rows emerge grouped by keyword id 4,4,4,5,5,6,7,8.
kubectl ... -tAc "EXPLAIN SELECT a.id, a.author FROM authors_author a INNER JOIN resources_resource_authors r ON a.id=r.author_id WHERE r.resource_id = 3;" -> 'Hash Join / -> Seq Scan on authors_author a / -> Hash -> Seq Scan on resources_resource_authors r' — the lookup table is the outer relation, which is why lookup-id order falls out.

corrections.field: anomaly #5 — 'the one place the two candidate orderings disagree' / 'it is the only row where the two disagree'
corrections.problem: The spec states twice that legacy_id 3's authors are the ONLY case where join-id order and the order production renders diverge, and tells a human to sign off on that single row. Wrong: KEYWORDS diverge on three of the six resources (3, 5 and 7), and organisations diverge on resource 6. An importer built to the spec will silently reorder the keyword list on half the library while the reviewer is told only one row moves.
corrections.fix: Expand the flag-for-human list and the post-import diff to cover every M2M on resources 3, 5, 6 and 7, not just resource 3's authors. Concretely, the pairs that change: r3 authors (Nilay Dogulu,Koen Verbist,Annelies Mertens -> Koen Verbist,Annelies Mertens,Nilay Dogulu); r3 keywords (citizen science,Open Science,Open Hydrology -> Open Science,Open Hydrology,citizen science); r5 keywords (citizen science,guide,data -> data,citizen science,guide); r7 keywords (citizen science,education,blue education,blue schools -> education,blue education,blue schools,citizen science); r6 organisations (5,27 -> 27,5, moot because _enrich re-sorts by name ASC).
corrections.evidence:
Join-id order: kubectl ... -tAc "SELECT rk.id||'|r='||rk.resource_id||'|k='||rk.keyword_id||'|'||k.keyword FROM resources_resource_keywords rk JOIN resources_keyword k ON k.id=rk.keyword_id ORDER BY rk.resource_id, rk.id;" -> r3: 5->kw5 Open Science, 6->kw6 Open Hydrology, 7->kw4 citizen science; r5: 9->kw8 data, 10->kw4 citizen science, 11->kw7 guide; r7: 13->kw9 education, 15->kw11 blue education, 16->kw12 blue schools, 17->kw4 citizen science.
Lookup-id order (what the site renders): the unordered probe above returns 4,5,6 for r3 and 4,7,8 for r5.
Orgs: kubectl ... -tAc "SELECT ro.id||'|r='||ro.resource_id||'|o='||ro.organisation_id FROM resources_resource_organisation ro ORDER BY ro.resource_id, ro.id;" -> 7|r=6|o=27 then 8|r=6|o=5.

corrections.field: resources_resource_audience anomaly impact — 'account for 6 of the 14 links' and field note '14 of the 14 links would get a wrong term'
corrections.problem: Both numbers are wrong, and they overstate the blast radius by 3x. Only audience ids 2, 5 and 6 are both in use and mismatched (audience 1, the fourth mismatch, is unused), and those three account for 5 links, not 6. The field-level note's '14 of the 14 links would get a wrong term from naive slugification' is flatly false — 9 of the 14 links point at audiences 3, 4 and 7, whose constants term IS the slug of their label.

corrections.field: resources_resource."dateUploaded" — 'Differs from dateCreated by 3ms-440ms' and the stated provenance
corrections.problem: Two defects. (1) The delta is signed and the spec hides the sign: dateUploaded is EARLIER than dateCreated on all six rows, so an importer or assertion written as 'uploaded >= created' fails on every row. (2) The stated provenance — 'resources/forms.py:394 sets dateUploaded=datetime.now() in the same save that sets auto_now_add dateCreated' — cannot hold for legacy ids 2 and 3, whose dateUploaded has ZERO microseconds while their dateCreated does not. datetime.now() does not produce whole-second timestamps; those two values came in through a different path (a form field or a backfill).
corrections.fix: State the delta as 'dateUploaded precedes dateCreated by 3ms to 440ms on all six rows', and soften the provenance to 'forms.py:394 is the path for the rows created through the public form; legacy ids 2 and 3 were written by some other path (whole-second timestamps)'. The mapping decision — extras, not a column — is unaffected.
corrections.evidence:
kubectl ... -tAc "SELECT id||' | up='||\"dateUploaded\"::text||' | cr='||\"dateCreated\"::text||' | delta='||(\"dateUploaded\"-\"dateCreated\")::text FROM resources_resource ORDER BY id;" ->

missed_anomalies.what: Three Django resource filters have no equivalent in the c4w ListingSpec, and two more changed from label-matching to slug-matching. The spec's open_questions raise only the category case, so four other inbound-link breaks go unrecorded — and one of them fails OPEN rather than closed.
missed_anomalies.impact: Three distinct behaviours. (1) `?license=CC+BY` FAILS OPEN — logic/query.py::_apply_native_filters only iterates keys declared in native_filters, so an undeclared 'license' param is dropped silently and the visitor gets the full unfiltered list believing it is filtered. That is worse than the category case, which at least returns zero. (2) `?theme=Best%20practices` and `?audience=Educators` return zero rows, because the term column holds 'best-practices'/'educators'. (3) The 13 imported keyword term_links are unreachable from the search box; 'blue schools' happens to still find legacy_id 7 only because the phrase also occurs in its abstract.
missed_anomalies.handling: Add these to the open_questions alongside category, since they are the same decision. Minimum viable answer: have the view coerce a label-shaped value to normalise_term() before it reaches _apply_term_facets (covers theme, audience and, with c4w_category.text, category), and either declare a 'license' ilike filter or explicitly reject unknown query params instead of ignoring them. Either way the import itself is unchanged — but the spec should not certify the resource surface as a faithful port while four filters silently changed meaning.

missed_anomalies.what: c4w_media_map has NO consumer in the extension: no /media/<path> route exists, and the migrate package is empty. The spec's raw-vs-percent-encoded decision is justified by a redirect that has not been written.

grep -rn 'media' --include=*.py /home/pabrojast/Proyectos/ckan-c4w/ckanext/c4w/ (excluding __pycache__) returns hits only in db.py (the table definition and its docstring, lines 367-379) and cli.py:46 (a row-count listing). blueprint.py registers project/organisation/resource/training_resource/event/post routes and a post_legacy_dated route — no media rule. ls -la ckanext/c4w/migrate/ -> only a 0-byte __init__.py.
The Django side is real: core_code/settings/base.py:38 sets MEDIA_URL = '/citizens4water/media/' (line 29 is the '/media/' default it overrides).
missed_anomalies.impact: The spec instructs 'store c4w_media_map.legacy_path as the raw unencoded column value, because that is the key the importer's idempotency check AND the redirect route both look up.' Half of that justification does not exist yet, so nothing in the codebase pins the encoding convention. If the redirect is written later by someone who percent-encodes the incoming path before the lookup, every one of the three space-bearing paths misses its row and the old image URLs 404 — the exact breakage the table was created to prevent.

But restate the justification honestly and add a note that whoever implements /citizens4water/media/<path:legacy_path> must url-unquote the incoming segment before querying c4w_media_map. Record it as a target-side prerequisite of the image import rather than an existing contract.

corrections.problem: The central anomaly's MECHANISM and EVIDENCE are wrong. The spec claims sanitize_html() 'fuses sentences together' producing 'ecosystems.OTTERS', and proves it with a SQL regexp_replace simulation. regexp_replace is not bleach. With the real bleach 6.4.0 that setup.py declares, bleach.clean(strip=True) emits a NEWLINE where a stripped block element stood. Measured on the real rows: id=6 -> '...reshwater ecosystems.\nOTTERS wishes to n...' (1 newline), id=3 -> '...for the community.\nThe vision for the...' (2 newlines). No fusion occurs. In practice this writes NULL for every row; logic/action/events.py::_enrich will always return main_organisation=None after import.

anomalies.what: events_event.approved is NOT the flag production uses to hide events. The real public filter is the events_unapprovedevents table, and it is empty — so nothing is hidden on the live site, including the one row whose boolean says approved=false.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FROM events_unapprovedevents -> 0; SELECT count(*) FROM events_approvedevents -> 0. events/views.py:56-62 reads `unApprovedEvents = UnApprovedEvents.objects.values_list('event_id', flat=True)` then `if not user.is_staff: events = events.exclude(id__in=unApprovedEvents)` — the exclusion is on the TABLE, never on the boolean, and it is applied ONLY to the upcoming queryset, not to ongoingEvents or pastEvents (views.py:42-44). The staff badge in themes/citizens4water/templates/events/_events_card.html:81 likewise tests `{% if event.id in approvedEvents %}`. Meanwhile SELECT approved, count(*) FROM events_event GROUP BY approved -> true=12, false=1; the false row is id=6 'CS4Water Conference 2025' (featured=true, url=https://cs4water.net/, end_date=2025-06-05 00:00+00, i.e. a past event, which the Django filter never touched at all).
anomalies.impact: logic/query.py:73-74 `_public_filter` does `query.filter(model_cls.approved.is_(True))` and _common.is_visible sets `published = bool(row.approved)`. A verbatim copy of the boolean therefore makes id=6 vanish from the new events listing and 404 on its detail page, even though it is publicly visible on ihp-wins today and is one of only two featured events. c4w_event has no `hidden` and no `moderated` column, so `approved` is the entire visibility decision — there is no second flag to soften the mistake.
anomalies.handling: Import approved=TRUE for all 13 rows (production parity) and stash the raw Django boolean in extras.legacy_approved. Do not try to reconstruct moderation state from events_approvedevents/events_unapprovedevents — both are empty. Flag id=6 to the C4W admins so a human decides whether it should stay published rather than the importer deciding silently.

anomalies.what: The approved and featured booleans are bound-but-unrendered fields on both the public create and edit forms, so every save through /citizens4water/editEvent/<pk>/ silently resets them to False.
anomalies.evidence: events/forms.py:88 `class Meta: model = Event; exclude = ['creator']` — only creator is excluded, so `approved` and `featured` are bound ModelForm fields. Grepping the rendered fields shows neither template outputs them: new_event.html renders form.title,url,description,language,start_date,end_date,hour,timezone,event_type,latitude,longitude,place,country,project,mainOrganisation,organisations (16 fields, no approved, no featured); editEvent.html renders the same 16. A ModelForm BooleanField for a non-null Django BooleanField is required=False, so an absent POST key cleans to False. Meanwhile the AJAX toggles (views.py::setFeaturedEvent, setApprovedOrUnapprovedEvent) do a full event.save(), so whichever action ran last wins.
anomalies.impact: It means the boolean has no stable meaning: it records whichever of 'an admin toggled it' or 'somebody re-saved the form' happened most recently, not a moderation decision. An importer that treats it as a reviewer verdict — or that later writes it back through a similar form — will keep corrupting it.
anomalies.handling: Reinforces the previous item: do not read the Django boolean as a moderation verdict. In ckanext-c4w keep approval out of the public event form entirely (the moderation routes own it), so the new form cannot reproduce the reset.

anomalies.what: hour is NULL on 10 of 13 rows that nonetheless carry a non-midnight time-of-day in start_date, and the Django card shows a time ONLY from hour. Where hour is set it is exactly the UTC time-of-day of start_date, so it duplicates the instant — but its NULLness is real information.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE hour IS NOT NULL) -> 2; count(*) FILTER (WHERE hour IS NULL AND (start_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::time <> '00:00:00') -> 10; count(*) FILTER (WHERE hour IS NULL AND (start_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::time = '00:00:00') -> 1. For the two rows that have it: id=12 hour=11:00:00 / start_utc_time=11:00:00 / start_local_time(Europe/Brussels)=12:00:00; id=14 hour=15:00:00 / start_utc_time=15:00:00 / start_local_time=16:00:00 — so `hour = (start_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::time` is TRUE and `hour = (start_date AT TIME ZONE timezone)::time` is FALSE for both. The rendering is _events_card.html:17-18: `{{event.start_date | date:" M d, Y"}}` (date only, the time component is never printed) followed by `{% if event.hour %}{{event.hour | time:'H:i'}} {% if event.timezone %}{{event.timezone}}{% endif %}{% endif %}`. The times sitting unseen in start_date are clearly boilerplate: SELECT to_char(start_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC','HH24:MI'), count(*) -> 06:00 x6, 09:00 x2, 12:00 x2, 11:00 x1, 15:00 x1, 00:00 x1; end times -> 18:00 x7, 12:00 x3, 17:00 x2, 00:00 x1.
anomalies.impact: A c4w event template that formats start_date with a time (the obvious thing to do, since c4w_event.start_date is a DateTime and hour looks redundant) would publish a start time for 10 events that no author ever entered and that the Django site has never shown — e.g. 'The Great UK WaterBlitz Autumn 2026, 06:00'. Conversely, an importer that decides hour is redundant and drops it loses the only published start times on the site (ids 12 and 14).
anomalies.handling: Import hour verbatim into c4w_event.hour, NULLs included, and make the event templates render a time if and only if hour is not NULL — exactly the {% if event.hour %} guard Django uses. Treat start_date's time-of-day as internal ordering data only, never as display.

anomalies.what: events_event.timezone is a display label that Django never applies to start_date/end_date, and 9 of 13 rows still hold the untouched model default Europe/Brussels — including events in Abu Dhabi, Dublin and the UK.
anomalies.evidence: core_code/settings/base.py:69-72 set TIME_ZONE = "UTC" and USE_TZ = True, and MIDDLEWARE (base.py:126) contains no timezone-activating middleware, so Django renders every datetime in UTC. The template prints the string beside hour, it never converts (_events_card.html:18). Distinct values measured: Europe/Brussels(9), Australia/Melbourne(1), Europe/Helsinki(1), Europe/Paris(1), US/Central(1). Places vs declared zone: id=21 place='Abu Dhabi' tz='Europe/Brussels' (start_utc 2026-12-08 06:00 -> 'as declared tz' 07:00, but Abu Dhabi is UTC+4); id=19 place='Dublin' tz='Europe/Brussels' (09:00 UTC -> 11:00, Ireland is UTC+1 in October); id=17 place='England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland' tz='Europe/Brussels' (06:00 UTC -> 08:00, UK is UTC+1 in September); id=6 and id=16 place='Delft' with tz Europe/Paris and Europe/Brussels respectively (same offset as Europe/Amsterdam, harmless). All 5 values ARE valid IANA names: each joined a row in pg_timezone_names, each constructs under Python zoneinfo.ZoneInfo, and each is in pytz.common_timezones (pytz 2026.2) — 'US/Central' is a tzdb backward-compat link but resolves everywhere tested.
anomalies.impact: An importer or template that does `start_date.astimezone(ZoneInfo(timezone))` to 'fix up' local times would shift 3 events by 1–3 hours into times nobody entered, and would silently rebase 9 events onto a default zone that describes only the platform's Brussels office, not the event. The naming trap is that the column looks authoritative and every value is a valid IANA zone, so nothing throws.
anomalies.handling: Store timezone verbatim in c4w_event.timezone and use it only as the label printed next to hour, exactly as Django does. Store start_date/end_date as naive UTC. Never call astimezone with this value. If the new UI ever wants true local times, that is a data-entry fix, not an import transform.

anomalies.what: The one event with coordinates has a longitude outside the valid range, and neither Postgres nor the target schema will reject it.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT id, latitude, longitude, latitude BETWEEN -90 AND 90, longitude BETWEEN -180 AND 180 FROM events_event WHERE latitude IS NOT NULL OR longitude IS NOT NULL -> a single row: id=6, lat=76.830808, lon=-393.439019, lat_ok=true, lon_ok=FALSE. Wrapping it back into range gives ((lon+180) mod 360)-180 = -33.439019 — the signature of a Leaflet map panned past the antimeridian, consistent with new_event.html:143-144 which does `$("#id_latitude").val(parseFloat(lat).toFixed(6))` with no normalisation. The row's own place is 'Delft' (roughly 52.01N, 4.36E), so even the wrapped coordinate (76.83N, 33.44W, in the Greenland Sea) is wrong. The other 12 rows have both columns NULL.
anomalies.impact: Django's numeric(9,6) accepted it and c4w_event.latitude/longitude are the same types.Numeric(9,6), so a verbatim copy imports clean and only fails later — in a Leaflet/GeoJSON layer, in a bbox query, or in a distance calculation — with no error at import time to point at.
anomalies.handling: Validate on import: wrap longitude into [-180,180] and require latitude in [-90,90]; if either fails after wrapping, write NULL for BOTH columns rather than half a coordinate. For this row the honest outcome is NULL/NULL plus a flagged report line, because the wrapped value is still not Delft. Add the range check to the c4w event form validator too, since the same Leaflet widget is being ported.

anomalies.what: events_event.country is free-text English country NAMES from Nominatim, not ISO codes — unlike every other country field on the platform — and two of the eight values are not countries at all.
anomalies.evidence: Column definition: `country character varying(50)` (information_schema) and events/models.py:52 `country = models.CharField(max_length=50, blank=True, null=True)` — a plain CharField. It is filled by JS: new_event.html:148 requests `https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/reverse?...&accept-language=en` and line 258 assigns `data?.address?.country` into the hidden input; Nominatim's alpha-2 `address.country_code` is available in that same response but is never captured. Exact stored values: 'Australia'(1), 'Belgium'(1), 'England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland'(1), 'Ireland'(1), 'Netherlands'(1), 'the Netherlands'(1), 'United Arab Emirates'(1), 'Worldwide'(1), NULL(5), '' (0). Contrast the same-named column on organisations, which is a django_countries.CountryField: SELECT country, count(*) FROM organisations_organisation GROUP BY country -> AT, BE, BO, CH, DE, ES, GB, GT, IN, IT, KE, LV, ML, NL, US and 5 empty — all alpha-2. Running text.normalise_term over the event values yields 'australia', 'belgium', 'england-wales-scotland-and-northern-ireland', 'ireland', 'netherlands', 'the-netherlands', 'united-arab-emirates', 'worldwide'.
anomalies.impact: The 'country' vocabulary in c4w is documented as holding ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 terms (constants.py:279-282) and helpers.c4w_country_name feeds the term straight to Babel as a code. Writing normalise_term(country) into it would (a) split one country across two facet values — 'netherlands' and 'the-netherlands' are the same country typed twice; (b) create the non-country facets 'worldwide' and 'england-wales-scotland-and-northern-ireland'; (c) make c4w_country_name miss on every one of them, so the facet renders the raw slug next to real codes rendered as 'Belgium'; and (d) pollute the shared vocabulary that organisations and projects populate correctly with codes.
anomalies.handling: Two targets from one column. (1) c4w_event.country keeps the string verbatim (db.py:314-316 explicitly reserves it for this). (2) Emit a c4w_term_link 'country' row ONLY on an exact match against an English territory-name table after case-folding and stripping a leading 'the ' — that resolves 6 of 8: Australia->AU, Belgium->BE, Ireland->IE, Netherlands->NL, 'the Netherlands'->NL, United Arab Emirates->AE. Emit nothing for 'Worldwide' (not a country) and nothing automatic for 'England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland' (an enumeration of the UK's four constituent countries; GB is the right answer but no name lookup will produce it — put it in a hand-curated alias map or leave it unfaceted). Never fall back to normalise_term. Report every unresolved value rather than dropping it silently.

anomalies.what: 5 of 13 events have country NULL even though `place` names the country, so the country facet would cover fewer than half the events.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE country IS NULL) -> 5. Those rows are id=4 place='Oulu, Finland', id=15 place='Antwerp, Belgium', and ids 12, 13, 14 all place='Online'. So two of the five NULLs sit next to a place string that spells the country out, and three are genuinely placeless online events. Note also that Django's own country filter was never functional: events/views.py builds the `cwc` set and _finder_events.html:33-42 renders a country <select>, but applyFilters (views.py:146-176) handles only q, language, event_type, project and organisation — country is collected by setFilters and then never applied.
anomalies.impact: Only 6 of 13 events would get a country term even after the alias work above, and 2 of the 7 gaps are recoverable. Because the Django country filter never actually filtered, there is no production behaviour to compare against — nobody has ever noticed the gaps.
anomalies.handling: Do not parse `place` heuristically in the importer (a comma-split would turn 'England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland' into 'England'). Import the 6 resolvable terms, leave the rest unfaceted, and hand the C4W admins the 7-row gap list (ids 4, 15 recoverable as FI and BE; ids 12, 13, 14 genuinely online; ids 17, 18 need a human) to fix in the new form, which should capture Nominatim's country_code rather than its country name.

anomalies.what: events_event has no created or modified column at all — the table is 20 columns and none is a record timestamp — while c4w_event.created/.modified default to _utcnow.
anomalies.evidence: The full information_schema column list for events_event is id, title, description, description_en, place, country, start_date, end_date, hour, timezone, language, url, featured, event_type, latitude, longitude, approved, creator_id, mainOrganisation_id, project_id. db.py:332-333 declares Column('created', DateTime, default=_utcnow) and Column('modified', DateTime, default=_utcnow). The only real timestamps are in django_admin_log, and they cover 10 of 13 events: SELECT e.id FROM events_event e WHERE NOT EXISTS (admin-log row for it) -> 4, 5, 6.
anomalies.impact: Left to the defaults, all 13 events get the same import-run timestamp; any 'recently added' ordering or 'new' badge becomes meaningless, and a re-run of the importer would move every timestamp again unless created is written only on insert.
anomalies.handling: Backfill from django_admin_log (join django_content_type on app_label='events' AND model='event', object_id = id::text): created = min(action_time) where action_flag=1, modified = max(action_time). Values are listed in the field table above. For ids 4, 5, 6 there is no source — use the import timestamp and record extras.created_estimated=true so the three synthetic values are distinguishable. On re-runs, update `modified` but never overwrite an existing `created`.

anomalies.what: Both event creators have usernames CKAN itself would reject, and c4w_event.created_by is a CKAN user UUID, not a username.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT e.creator_id, count(*), u.name, u.email FROM events_event e LEFT JOIN authtools_user u ON u.id=e.creator_id GROUP BY ... -> creator 5 = 'Karen' (karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be, 6 events), creator 62 = 'Liza' (liza@rvo-society.be, 6 events), NULL (1 event, id=6). Both names contain uppercase: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE name<>lower(name)) FROM authtools_user -> 6 of 62 (Admin, Jorge, Karen, Jef, Jef, Liza). CKAN's own rule is ckan/logic/validators.py:375 `name_match = re.compile('[a-z0-9_\-]*$')` applied by name_validator (line 405), and lookups are exact-case: ckan/model/user.py:62-66 `query.filter(or_(cls.name == user_reference, cls.id == user_reference))`. The target is a UUID, not a name: logic/action/_common.py:68 `if getattr(row, 'created_by', None) and row.created_by == user.id`. Separately, 'Jef' is duplicated in authtools_user (ids 10 and 17) — not a creator of any event, but it shows Django's name column is not unique the way CKAN's is.
anomalies.impact: user_show('Karen') returns NotFound if the CKAN account is 'karen', so created_by lands NULL for 6 or even all 12 events; the author then cannot see their own row while it is unapproved, and 'my events' is empty. Worse, an importer that stores the raw string 'Karen' in created_by writes a value that never equals user.id and so silently fails the ownership check forever, with no error anywhere.
anomalies.handling: Resolve to a CKAN user.id through user_show, trying the name as stored, then lowercased, then the authtools_user.email; leave created_by NULL on a miss and always record extras.legacy_creator_username so the link is repairable. Never write a username into created_by. Never create a CKAN user. Report the two names ('Karen', 'Liza') for a human to confirm against the real CKAN accounts before the cutover — the assumption that Django usernames are CKAN usernames does not survive contact with these values.

anomalies.what: Every event-to-entity link in the events area is empty: project_id, mainOrganisation_id and the whole events_event_organisations join table.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE project_id IS NOT NULL) -> 0; count(*) FILTER (WHERE "mainOrganisation_id" IS NOT NULL) -> 0 (over all 13 rows). SELECT count(*) FROM events_event_organisations -> 0. All three are live features in Django: the fields are rendered on both forms (form.project, form.mainOrganisation, form.organisations in new_event.html:82-84 and editEvent.html:93-95) and the card renders pills for all three (_events_card.html:51-66).
anomalies.impact: The importer's FK-resolution and relation-writing code for events will execute zero times, so nothing about it is validated by the real data — including the camelCase quoting of "mainOrganisation_id", which is the kind of thing that only fails once someone finally links an event. logic/action/events.py::_enrich will return project=None and main_organisation=None for all 13 rows, so any template branch behind those will be dead on day one.
anomalies.handling: Still implement all three mappings (single-valued FKs to the native indexed columns c4w_event.project_id / main_organisation_id per the design rule; the M2M to c4w_relation predicate 'organisation'), but cover them with synthetic fixtures in tests/test_import_mapping.py rather than trusting a production dry run to exercise them. Remember to quote "mainOrganisation_id" in every raw SQL read.

anomalies.what: description_en duplicates description byte-for-byte on all 13 rows, so on THIS table the base column is the safe source — but the descriptions are summernote HTML whose styling the c4w sanitizer strips, and one row has no markup at all.
anomalies.evidence:
SELECT id, length(description), length(description_en), description = description_en FROM events_event -> all 13 rows have equal lengths and equal=true; description_en is NULL on 0 rows. events/translation.py registers Event with fields=('description',) only, and events_event has exactly one shadow column (SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name LIKE 'events_%' AND column_name LIKE '%\_en' -> events_event.description_en, events_helptext.title_en, events_helptext.paragraph_en). Content check: 12 of 13 match '<[a-zA-Z/]' and contain

; 6 contain style=; 2 contain  ; 0 contain
anomalies.impact: Two separate traps. (1) The base/shadow choice is a coin flip here because they agree, so a mapping that guesses works on events and may be wrong elsewhere — pick deliberately. (2) sanitize.ALLOWED_TAGS has no 'span' and ALLOWED_ATTRS is {'a': [...]} only, so every style= and every <span> is stripped; that is intended, but the tag-free row id=6 then renders as one unwrapped block with no paragraph, visually unlike the other twelve.
anomalies.handling:
Take the base column `description` (it is NOT NULL; the shadow is nullable) and drop description_en. Run sanitize_html on it, and after sanitising, if the result contains no block tag, wrap it in

...

so id=6 renders consistently. Do not attempt to preserve the inline styles — losing them is the point of the allowlist.

anomalies.what: Slug source is title (there is no Django slug column and no Django event detail URL), so the 13 c4w event slugs are all new URLs. No collisions, but one is truncated mid-word.
anomalies.evidence: events_event has no slug column (full column list above), and events/urls.py defines only new_event/, events/, editEvent/<int:pk>/, deleteEvent/<int:pk>/, setFeaturedEvent/, setApprovedEvent/ — no per-event page exists to preserve. SELECT duplicate titles -> none; duplicate urls -> none. Running ckanext.c4w.text.slugify over the 13 real titles in-process produced 13 distinct slugs, so unique_slug never needs a -2 suffix. Only id=16 exceeds the 90-char cap: a 116-char title becomes 'developing-stakeholder-driven-solutions-for-a-water-resilient-river-basin-management-conne' (cut inside 'connecting'). id=15's 'Shaping Sustainable Futures: Global Challenges, (G)local Solutions?' becomes 'shaping-sustainable-futures-global-challenges-g-local-solutions'. Titles are also editable after creation — django_admin_log shows id=14 renamed from 'Webinar Citizen Science meets Water' to 'Launch webinar Citizens4Water' and id=21 from 'UN Water Conference' to '2026 UN Water Conference'.
anomalies.impact: Low risk of breakage (no legacy URL to keep, no collisions), but the truncated slug for id=16 is a permanent public URL, and db.unique_slug's docstring is explicit that a slug is assigned once and never moved on rename — so whatever the importer writes on the first run is the address forever.
anomalies.handling: Generate slugs with db.unique_slug(C4wEvent, title) and make the FIRST import run authoritative: re-running must match on legacy_id and leave the existing slug alone, never re-slugify from a possibly-edited title. Optionally hand-set id=16's slug to something shorter before the first run, since that is the only chance to choose it.

open_questions: events_event.approved: I recommend importing TRUE for all 13 because that is what the live site serves (events_unapprovedevents is empty and past/ongoing events were never filtered), but this is a publishing decision, not a data one. Does C4W want id=6 'CS4Water Conference 2025' (featured=true, past, external url live) published in the new portal, or genuinely unapproved?

constants.MODERATED_ENTITY_TYPES includes 'event', but c4w_event has no `moderated` and no `hidden` column (unlike c4w_project and c4w_resource, which have both). So 'never reviewed' and 'reviewed and rejected' are indistinguishable for events, and a rejected event cannot be hidden without also un-approving it. Is that intentional, or should c4w_event gain `moderated`?

CKAN username resolution needs confirmation before the cutover: are the real CKAN accounts 'Karen'/'Liza' or 'karen'/'liza'? CKAN's own name_validator (ckan/logic/validators.py:375) forbids uppercase, so accounts with these exact names should not exist — yet the Django backend copied them verbatim from CKAN's user_login response (themes/citizens4water/backends/ckanlogin.py:50). One of those two things is wrong and only a query against the CKAN database can say which. I did not query the CKAN production context.

'England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland' (id=17, in BOTH place and country) should almost certainly facet as GB, but no name lookup produces that. Do we want a hand-curated alias map in the importer (which then needs an owner), or should the row simply carry no country term?

events_event.language is 'EN' for all 13 rows, so nothing in the data distinguishes a column from the 'language' free vocabulary. I mapped it to the native column (single-valued CharField, per the design rule) and lowercased it to 'en' for parity with resources_resource."inLanguage". But the platform is inconsistent across areas — resources store codes ('en'), projects use a projects_language table of NAMES ('English', 'Australian English') — so the shared 'language' vocabulary already has two term shapes. Someone should decide the canonical form before events, projects and resources all write into it.
Django's LANGUAGE_CHOICES includes 'OT' (Other), which is not an ISO 639-1 code. It occurs 0 times today, so the importer needs no rule — but the new event form does. What should 'Other' store?

corrections.problem: The spec describes it as an unconstrained CharField. It is a Django choices field, and the model and the form disagree about the choice set: the model binds choices to pytz.common_timezones while the form overrides it with a ChoiceField over pytz.all_timezones. Django enforces choices only in form/model validation, never at the DB level, so the column can legally hold any string an admin writes.
corrections.fix: Note the choices binding and the model/form divergence. Practical consequence for the importer: do not assume the stored value is in common_timezones - it is only guaranteed to be in all_timezones, and not even that if it was written through the admin or raw SQL. Keep the recommended handling (store verbatim, never astimezone). All five values in this data are in fact valid: I confirmed each constructs under zoneinfo.ZoneInfo and each is in both pytz.common_timezones and pytz.all_timezones with pytz 2026.2, including the backward-compat link US/Central.

missed_anomalies.what: psycopg2 returns timestamptz as a tz-aware datetime rendered in the CONNECTION's TimeZone, so 'read as UTC and store naive UTC' is only correct if the importer forces the session timezone. The spec states the outcome but never states the mechanism, and a naive .replace(tzinfo=None) on a non-UTC connection shifts every event.
missed_anomalies.evidence: SHOW timezone; -> Etc/UTC (so the values quoted throughout the spec are UTC by luck of the server default). Then: SET TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'; SELECT id, start_date::text FROM events_event WHERE id IN (4,6,21); -> 4|2026-03-02 07:00:00-05, 21|2026-12-08 01:00:00-05, 6|2025-06-02 20:00:00-04. Nothing raises. The failure is invisible at import time and only shows up as events listed on the wrong day.
missed_anomalies.handling: Have the importer either execute SET TIME ZONE 'UTC' on the legacy connection before reading, or convert explicitly with value.astimezone(datetime.timezone.utc).replace(tzinfo=None). Assert on at least one known row (id=21 start_date must be 2026-12-08T06:00:00) before writing anything.

fields.django_type: timestamp with time zone NOT NULL (author-set, NOT auto_now_add)
fields.target: c4w_post.created_on, and use the same value to seed c4w_post.created
fields.transform: AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' -> naive UTC datetime

Four rows carry a hand-set 12:00:00 time (ids 2,3,4,5) — these were backdated by an editor, which is why the column is not auto_now_add. Seed c4w_post.created from it too, otherwise 'Most Recent Created' would order by import time.

fields.django_type: timestamp with time zone NOT NULL, models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)
fields.nullable_in_practice: 0/16 NULL. Range 2025-07-03 .. 2026-06-30. updated_on >= created_on in 16/16 rows (count of updated_on < created_on = 0), and never exactly equal.
fields.target: c4w_post.updated_on, and use the same value to seed c4w_post.modified
fields.transform: AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' -> naive UTC datetime
fields.notes: auto_now=True means Django rewrote this on every save, so it reflects the last EDIT, not the publication date. Write it explicitly; do not let c4w's own _utcnow() default fill it, and seed c4w_post.modified from it so 'Most Recent Updated' ordering matches the legacy site.

fields.django_type: integer NOT NULL, models.IntegerField(choices=STICKY=((0,'No'),(1,'Yes')), default=0). NO CHECK constraint in the database.
fields.nullable_in_practice: 0/16 NULL. SELECT sticky, count(*) GROUP BY sticky -> only one group: 0|16. Value 1 does not occur.
fields.transform: bool(x) i.e. sticky != 0 -> False for all 16 rows
fields.notes: LOSSLESS for the current data, because only the value 0 exists. The Django choices are two-valued so the Boolean target is right in principle, but the column is a bare integer with no CHECK constraint, so the importer should still assert sticky IN (0,1) and fail loudly rather than silently truncating an unexpected value to True. Consequence to state up front: nothing in production is pinned, so the 'Pinned' badge in post_card.html and the m.sticky.desc() lead in the ordering are both no-ops after import — that is fidelity, not a lost pin.

fields.django_type: integer NOT NULL, models.IntegerField(choices=STATUS=((0,'Draft'),(1,'Publish')), default=0). NO CHECK constraint.
fields.nullable_in_practice: 0/16 NULL. SELECT status, count(*) GROUP BY status -> 0|1 and 1|15.
fields.transform: {0: u'draft', 1: u'published'} — map from the INTEGER, never from the Django choice label
fields.notes: CONFIRMED from the data: exactly one row has status=0 (id=1, 'Test New', slug 'test-new', a Lorem-ipsum test post by author 1) and 15 have status=1, matching the brief's '15 published'. Django's PostList queryset filters status=1 and post_detail does get_object_or_404(status=1), so 1 == publicly visible. The c4w side compares against the literal u'published' in query.py:78 (_public_filter) and _common.py:59. See the 'Publish' vs 'published' anomaly — this mapping is the one place the importer can silently blank the whole news section.

anomalies.what: sanitize_rich_html silently deletes 17 inline and 2 YouTube
anomalies.evidence:
Tag census: SELECT lower(m[1]), count(*), count(DISTINCT id) FROM (SELECT id, regexp_matches(content,'<\s*([a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*)','g') AS m FROM blog_post) s GROUP BY 1 -> img|17|6, iframe|2|2. Running the REAL function (bleach 6.4.0, importlib-loaded ckanext/c4w/logic/sanitize.py) over all 16 bodies gives before/after tag counts img 17->0, iframe 2->0. Affected posts: SELECT id, slug, imgs, iframes FROM blog_post WHERE content ~* ' 3(6 imgs), 4(3), 5(2), 8(2), 12(2), 13(2), 6(1 iframe), 15(1 iframe). All 19 srcs enumerated: 17 are /citizens4water/media/django-summernote//., 2 are https://www.youtube.com/embed/n18INiq6tGw and https://www.youtube.com/embed/u0wTVu4Jl74?si=fxl0HSe7bKSniYHx. Concrete before/after on post 13: '


' becomes '


' — an empty paragraph.
anomalies.impact: A naive importer runs sanitize_rich_html, reports success, and 8 of 15 published posts quietly lose every in-body illustration and both video embeds. Total prose is unchanged (measured: per-post extracted-text delta is 0 for 14 of 16 rows and -4/-1 chars on the other two), so no length check, no diff on word count and no smoke test will catch it. It is only visible by looking at the rendered page.
anomalies.handling: Do not let the import be the moment this is decided. (1) Upload the 17 summernote files into c4w_media_map regardless — they are needed by the /citizens4water/media/<path> redirect anyway. (2) Write a manifest to c4w_post.extras.inline_media = [{legacy_path, new_url, original_name, ordinal}] so the association survives losslessly whatever the body ends up containing. (3) Escalate the allowlist question as a product decision, not an importer default: either add 'img' to RICH_ALLOWED_TAGS with RICH_ALLOWED_ATTRS['img']=['src','alt'] plus a validator pinning src to the portal's own upload host (which is exactly the 'unvalidated second image ingress' the docstring refuses, so it needs the host check to be acceptable), or render the manifest as a figure gallery beneath the body from extras. For the 2 YouTube embeds, substitute a plain <a href> to the watch URL during the rewrite pass, BEFORE sanitizing, so the link survives as an anchor instead of vanishing. Whichever is chosen, the import must FAIL LOUDLY (or emit a per-post report) when a body loses an img or iframe, rather than proceeding silently.

anomalies.what: The inline images are a SECOND media population that exists only inside the HTML — there is no Django model column pointing at them. A media importer that walks the *_url/image columns of the six entity tables uploads 16 blog files and misses 17.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name LIKE '%summernote%' -> django_summernote_attachment, 34 rows. SELECT a.id, a.file, EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM blog_post p WHERE p.content LIKE '%'||a.file||'%') FROM django_summernote_attachment a -> exactly 17 true, 17 false. SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT m[1]) FROM (SELECT regexp_matches(content,'src="(/citizens4water/media/[^"]+)"','g') AS m FROM blog_post) s -> 17|17, so the referenced srcs are 1:1 with the referenced attachment rows, no file used twice.
anomalies.impact: Every one of the 17 rewritten would 404 after the Django host is decommissioned, and the /citizens4water/media/ redirect would have no c4w_media_map row to resolve. If instead the importer naively uploads all 34 attachment rows it wastes half the transfers on orphans from superseded edits (the entire 2025-07-03 batch of 13, plus ids 25, 26, 29, 31).
anomalies.handling: Drive the inline-media upload from a regex scan of blog_post.content for src="/citizens4water/media/...", not from the attachment table and not from the entity image columns. Join back to django_summernote_attachment on `file` only to recover the original filename for alt text. Strip the MEDIA_URL prefix ('/citizens4water/media/') before using the remainder as c4w_media_map.legacy_path, so the key matches the shape the redirect route resolves.

Readers see a photo credit naming a photographer with no photo, and h6 sub-headings become undifferentiated running text. h3 (8 occurrences, posts 4 and 13) survives because it is on the allowlist, so the same document ends up with some headings intact and some dissolved — which looks like a rendering bug rather than a policy.

In the pre-sanitize rewrite pass, promote
to
