anomalies.what: The Django display label for status=1 is 'Publish', not 'Published'. Deriving the c4w value from the label instead of the integer yields 'publish', which matches nothing.
anomalies.evidence: blog/models.py: STATUS = ((0, "Draft"), (1, "Publish")). The c4w side hard-codes the other spelling: query.py:78 `query.filter(model_cls.status == u'published')` inside _public_filter, and _common.py:59 `published = row.status == u'published'`. Data: SELECT status, count(*) FROM blog_post GROUP BY status -> 0|1, 1|15.
anomalies.impact: slugify(get_status_display()) or any label-driven mapping stores 'publish' on all 15 published rows. _public_filter then matches zero rows, so /citizens4water/blog renders an empty news section and every post detail 404s — with no error anywhere in the import log, because 'publish' is a perfectly valid string for an unconstrained UnicodeText column. Symmetrically, 'Draft' happens to slugify to the correct 'draft', so the one draft behaves correctly and masks the bug in any spot check that only looks at the draft.
anomalies.handling: Map from the INTEGER with an explicit, exhaustive dict {0: u'draft', 1: u'published'} and raise on any other value rather than defaulting. Add a post-import assertion that SELECT count(*) FROM c4w_post WHERE status='published' equals 15, since that number is known in advance.

anomalies.what: blog_post.image is a BARE filename with no directory component — the only image column in the entire legacy database that is not path-prefixed.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE image LIKE '%/%') FROM blog_post -> 0 (of 16). Compared against every other image-bearing column: projects_project.image1 38/38 contain '/', image2 29/29, image3 24/24, organisations_organisation.logo 30/30, resources_resource.image1 5/5, platforms_platform.logo 4/4. Cause confirmed in blog/models.py: image = models.ImageField(max_length=200, default='default_blog.png') — no upload_to, so files land in MEDIA_ROOT itself (settings/base.py: MEDIA_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'media', MEDIA_URL = '/citizens4water/media/'). Sample values: '5878303.jpg', 'AFR_EAU.png', 'Zaniel_April_from_GroundTruth_taking_a_water_sample_from_the_Mthinzima_wetland.JPEG'.
anomalies.impact: Any shared media helper that assumes a prefixed relative path — joining MEDIA_ROOT with a leading directory, deriving a bucket folder from the first segment, or splitting on '/' to classify the asset — mishandles all 16 blog headers. And because c4w_media_map.legacy_path is globally UNIQUE across all entities, a bare filename occupies the unprefixed namespace: a future blog upload named e.g. 'images' or colliding with another entity's basename would break the key. Case matters too: 13/16 filenames contain uppercase letters and 1/16 has an uppercase extension ('.JPEG'), so any lower()-ing of the path in the media pipeline produces a legacy_path that the /citizens4water/media/<path> redirect will never match.
anomalies.handling: Use the stored value verbatim and case-sensitively as c4w_media_map.legacy_path; resolve the source file as MEDIA_ROOT/<image> with no interposed directory. Do not normalise case anywhere in the media path pipeline. 0/16 rows use the 'default_blog.png' default, so the importer never has to decide whether to upload the placeholder — but it should still guard for it, since the column default means a future row could carry it.

anomalies.what: authtools_user.name is a display name, not a CKAN username, for the authors of 15 of the 16 posts. 'Admin' and 'Karen' cannot legally be CKAN usernames, so the author lookup fails on 94% of the blog.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT u.id,u.name,u.email,count(p.id) FROM authtools_user u JOIN blog_post p ON p.author_id=u.id GROUP BY 1,2,3 -> 1|Admin|jbarba@ibercivis.es|1, 5|Karen|karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be|14, 8|amertens|a.mertens@unesco.org|1. CKAN's rule (ckan/logic/validators.py:375) is name_match = re.compile('[a-z0-9_\-]*$') — 'purely lowercase alphanumeric (ascii) characters and these symbols: -_' — which 'Admin' and 'Karen' fail. Three independent confirmations that `name` is not a username here: (a) SELECT count(*) FROM authtools_user WHERE name ~ '[^a-z0-9_.-]' -> 6 rows (ids 1 Admin, 2 Jorge, 5 Karen, 10 Jef, 17 Jef, 62 Liza); (b) `name` is NOT unique — SELECT name,count(*) FROM authtools_user GROUP BY name HAVING count(*)>1 -> Jef|2 (ids 10,17), and \d+ authtools_user shows a UNIQUE constraint on email only, none on name; (c) the accounts differ in provenance — id=8 amertens has an EMPTY password, the signature of the CKAN backend's User.objects.get_or_create(name=user_info['name']) in themes/citizens4water/backends/ckanlogin.py, whereas ids 1 and 5 carry local pbkdf2_sha256 hashes, i.e. they were made with Django's own createsuperuser/admin before that backend existed.
anomalies.impact: An importer that trusts 'Django usernames ARE CKAN usernames' calls user_show(id='Karen') for 14 posts and user_show(id='Admin') for 1, gets 404 on both, and then either (a) crashes mid-import after the first 1-2 posts, (b) silently writes NULL author_id on 15 of 16 rows, or (c) violates the standing rule by creating CKAN users named 'Karen' and 'Admin' — which CKAN would reject anyway on name_validator, turning a data problem into a confusing validation error. Consequence of the NULL path: harmless for the 14 published Karen posts (no template renders a byline; post_detail.html shows only <time>, post_card.html shows date + Pinned badge), but NOT harmless for post id=1, the only draft — _common.py:60-70 grants draft visibility solely via `row.author_id == user.id`, so a NULL author makes that draft unreachable by every user including its own author, with no admin path to recover it.
anomalies.handling: Do not assume the identity holds; verify it per user before importing. Run a pre-flight that resolves each of the 3 distinct author names against CKAN via user_show and prints a table of name -> resolved/unresolved. On an unresolved author: write NULL to c4w_post.author_id, record extras.legacy_author_name and extras.legacy_author_email verbatim, and emit a WARN naming the post — never create the CKAN user. Supply an operator-editable override map {django_user_id: ckan_username} so the three real people can be wired to their actual CKAN accounts (the emails jbarba@ibercivis.es, karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be, a.mertens@unesco.org are the join key a human can resolve); email is the reliable identifier here, name is not. Note the same 6 bad names will hit projects/organisations/events creator and editor mappings, so the override map should be shared, not blog-local.

anomalies.what: Regenerating the slug from the title instead of reusing the stored one changes the URL of 2 of the 16 posts.
anomalies.evidence: Ran ckanext/c4w/text.py slugify(title) against all 16 stored slugs. Two diverge. id=3: stored (146 chars) 'guest-blog-from-environmental-justice-at-lake-titicaca-to-nature-based-solutions-at-lake-victoria-citizen-science-as-a-driver-of-social-innovation' vs slugify (90 chars) 'guest-blog-from-environmental-justice-at-lake-titicaca-to-nature-based-solutions-at-lake-v' — truncated by slugify's max_length=90 default. id=15: stored 'bridging-science-and-community-interview-with-afreau' vs slugify 'bridging-science-and-community-interview-with-afr-eau', because the title is 'Bridging Science and Community: Interview with AFR’EAU' with U+2019 RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK, which text.py deliberately turns into a SEPARATOR (documented in its own docstring) while Django's slugify deleted it. The stored slugs are already safe: count(*) FILTER (WHERE slug !~ '^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$') = 0, 16/16 distinct, no uppercase, no underscore.
anomalies.impact: Two published posts get new URLs, and every inbound link, share and search-engine result for them breaks — including through the legacy redirect, since post_legacy_dated() forwards on the slug alone (blueprint.py: 'the date carried no information the slug does not — blog_post.slug is already unique'). If the old slug is used to look up the row it 404s; if the new one is used the redirect target does not exist. The id=3 case is the worse of the two because a 90-char truncation is not visually obvious in a log.
anomalies.handling: Copy blog_post.slug verbatim into c4w_post.slug and never call db.unique_slug() for posts — the values are already unique and already URL-safe, so there is nothing for it to fix and everything for it to break. Assert 16 distinct slugs after insert. If slug regeneration is ever wanted for some other entity, note that text.slugify's 90-char cap is shorter than Django's SlugField(max_length=200) across the board, so it is a general truncation hazard, not a blog-specific one.

anomalies.what: All three modeltranslation shadow columns are byte-identical to their base columns in every row, so either can be read — but only the base columns are NOT NULL.
anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE title IS NOT DISTINCT FROM title_en), count(*) FILTER (WHERE content IS NOT DISTINCT FROM content_en), count(*) FILTER (WHERE excerpt IS NOT DISTINCT FROM excerpt_en) FROM blog_post -> 16|16|16. Also count(title_en)=count(content_en)=count(excerpt_en)=16, i.e. no shadow is NULL. Per-row lengths match exactly for all 16 rows in all three pairs. Confirmed intent in blog/translation.py: PostTranslationOptions fields = ('title','content','excerpt').
anomalies.impact: Low risk here, but the wrong instinct generalises badly. A COALESCE(x_en, x) is harmless; a COALESCE(x, x_en) is harmless; but reading ONLY the _en column is a latent NULL bug, since \d+ blog_post shows title_en/content_en/excerpt_en are all nullable while title/content/excerpt are NOT NULL. If a future row is created outside the modeltranslation-aware admin, the _en columns stay NULL and a shadow-first importer writes NULL into c4w_post.title, which is declared nullable=False and would abort the whole import.
anomalies.handling: Read the BASE columns (title, content, excerpt) and drop the three _en columns entirely. Do not write them to extras — there is no second language to preserve (MODELTRANSLATION_LANGUAGES=('en',)) and 16/16 rows prove the shadow adds nothing.

anomalies.what: Storing the excerpt as raw HTML poisons the c4w listing search, which runs ILIKE directly against the stored column.
anomalies.evidence:
posts.py declares search_columns=('title','excerpt','content') and query.py _apply_search builds getattr(model_cls, name).ilike(u'%%%s%%' % text) — a substring match on the raw column, no tag stripping. Measured false positives on the legacy excerpts: excerpt ILIKE '%color%' matches 4 posts but regexp_replace(excerpt,'<[^>]*>','','g') ILIKE '%color%' matches 0. Same shape for style 6/0, font 4/0, span 4/0, rgb 3/0, div 1/0, http 1/0. The markup is Wix-editor paste residue, e.g. id=3's excerpt begins '

'. Separately, striptags does not insert whitespace between blocks — markupsafe 3.0.3 Markup('

Alpha.

Beta.

').striptags() returns 'Alpha.Beta.' — and id=9 is the one excerpt with two

blocks (all other 15 have one or zero).
anomalies.impact: A visitor searching the news for 'color' or 'style' gets 4-6 hits whose visible text contains neither word, which reads as a broken search. And post 9's card renders two sentences fused without a space at the paragraph boundary.
anomalies.handling: Strip tags, unescape entities and collapse whitespace at IMPORT time, inserting a single space where block-level tags were, and store plain text in c4w_post.excerpt. This is display-lossless (post_card.html already applies | striptags and nothing renders it with | safe), removes the false positives, and fixes the id=9 fusion. Keep the original at extras.excerpt_html if a verbatim record is wanted. Note the same ILIKE-on-raw-HTML issue is unavoidable for content, which must stay HTML — that one has to be accepted, or fixed later with a separate plain-text search column.

anomalies.what: updated_on is auto_now=True, so it is a last-EDIT timestamp that bears no relation to publication, and c4w has two more timestamp columns that will silently default to import time if not written.
anomalies.evidence: blog/models.py: updated_on = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True); created_on = models.DateTimeField() (no auto_now_add — author-set). Measured: updated_on > created_on in 16/16 rows, never equal, gaps up to 13 months (id=2 created 2024-07-30, updated 2025-07-28; id=11 created 2026-02-11, updated 2026-03-23). Four rows carry a hand-set 12:00:00 created_on (ids 2,3,4,5), confirming editorial backdating. c4w_post declares FOUR datetime columns: created_on, updated_on, plus created and modified, the latter two with default=_utcnow.
anomalies.impact: If the importer writes only created_on and updated_on, the created/modified columns fill with the import timestamp — identical for all 16 rows. c4w_post's ix_c4w_post_public index is (status, sticky, created_on) and posts.py orders on created_on, so the public list stays correct; but any listing or admin view that falls back to the generic created/modified columns would show 16 posts all authored the same second, and 'Most Recent Updated' ordering would be arbitrary. Conversely, letting an ORM onupdate hook touch updated_on during import would overwrite the genuine editorial history with the migration date.
anomalies.handling: Write all four explicitly: created_on and created from blog_post.created_on; updated_on and modified from blog_post.updated_on. Convert with AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' — settings/base.py has USE_TZ=True and TIME_ZONE='UTC', so the timestamptz values are true UTC instants and the cast to c4w's naive types.DateTime is lossless. On a re-run (idempotency keyed on legacy_id) do not let modified drift to the re-run time, or every re-import silently reshuffles the 'Most Recent Updated' ordering.

open_questions: Do CKAN accounts exist for the two unresolvable authors? The dev postgres has no CKAN database to check against (SELECT datname FROM pg_database -> c4w_import, citizens4water, postgres, template*, template_postgis) and the production 'ckan' context is off-limits, so I could not test whether a lowercase 'karen'/'kverstraelen' or an admin account matches karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be (14 posts) and jbarba@ibercivis.es (1 draft). Someone with CKAN access should resolve these three emails to usernames before the import runs.

The allowlist decision is a product call, not an importer call, and it blocks 8 of 15 published posts. Options are: add 'img' to RICH_ALLOWED_TAGS with a src host-allowlist validator; render extras.inline_media as a figure gallery below the body; or accept the loss. sanitize.py's docstring argues against img on tracking-pixel grounds, but that reasoning assumes an arbitrary external src — every one of the 17 real srcs is on the portal's own media host, which the docstring's objection does not cover.

Should the single draft (id=1, 'Test New', slug 'test-new', Lorem ipsum body, author 'Admin') be imported at all? It is visibly a test row, and with an unresolvable author it would be invisible to everyone anyway. Importing it preserves legacy_id contiguity 1..16 and costs nothing; skipping it makes the row-count assertion cleaner. Recommend importing it as draft and flagging it for manual deletion.

Are the 17 orphaned django_summernote_attachment files still on disk, and should they be uploaded for the /citizens4water/media/<path> redirect even though nothing links to them? I could verify the reference status from SQL but not filesystem presence for any of the 34 files, nor for the 16 blog header images. A pre-flight existence check over MEDIA_ROOT is needed before the media pass, since a missing source file would otherwise leave image_url NULL with no distinction from 'not yet uploaded'.

The two YouTube iframes (posts 6 and 15) need a substitution shape decided: a bare <a href> to the watch URL, a link with a thumbnail, or an oEmbed-style server-rendered card. The rewrite has to happen before sanitizing either way, but only the first option needs no new allowlist entries.

verdict.area: Blog post (blog_post, django_summernote_attachment) — Django → ckanext-c4w c4w_post

corrections.problem: The spec invokes an existing "/citizens4water/media/<path> redirect" four separate times as load-bearing justification: to upload the 17 orphan attachments ("they are needed by the redirect anyway"), to forbid case-normalisation ("a legacy_path the redirect will never match"), and to choose the legacy_path shape ("so the key matches the shape the redirect route resolves"). That route does not exist. blueprint.py registers no media rule at all; the only occurrence of the string anywhere in the extension is an aspirational comment in db.py:370. Recommendations resting on it are unfounded today.
corrections.fix: State it as a PLANNED route (db.py's docstring), and list "implement the /citizens4water/media/ redirect" as an explicit prerequisite of the media pass. Re-justify the surviving recommendations on their own terms: case-sensitivity is required because MEDIA_ROOT is a case-sensitive filesystem holding real .JPEG files (blog_post id=12, summernote 2026-03-23 batch), not because of a redirect; the 17 REFERENCED attachments must be uploaded because the rewritten needs them; the 17 ORPHANS have NO justification left and should default to not-uploaded until the route exists.
corrections.evidence: grep -n "media" ckanext/c4w/blueprint.py -> 0 hits. grep -rn "media_map|MediaMap|/media/" over the whole extension -> only db.py:370 (a comment), db.py:372-379 (the table), db.py:437/471 (class+mapper), cli.py:46 (a count), tests/test_db_behavior.py:77. No add_url_rule mentions media. ckanext/c4w/migrate/ contains only an empty __init__.py, so no importer exists yet either.

corrections.problem: The spec justifies seeding c4w_post.modified with "so 'Most Recent Updated' ordering matches the legacy site", and anomaly 10 repeats it ("'Most Recent Updated' ordering would be arbitrary"). Both halves are false. (a) There is no 'modified'/'updated' ordering for posts: posts.py spec() declares orderings={'created': [m.sticky.desc(), m.created_on.desc().nullslast()], 'title': [m.title.asc()]} only, and query.py:270-272 silently coerces any unrecognised order to spec.default_order, so ?order=modified on /blog resolves to 'created'. The DEFAULT_ORDERINGS entry ('modified','Most Recent Updated') is never even advertised for posts, because posts.py get_actions() registers only c4w_post_show and c4w_post_list — make_facets is never built for this entity. (b) The legacy site never ordered by updated_on either: blog/views.py PostList queryset is .filter(status=1).order_by('-sticky','-created_on').
corrections.fix: Keep the action (write all four datetimes explicitly) but replace the reason. The real reason is that c4w_post.modified/created default to _utcnow, so leaving them unwritten stamps all 16 rows with the same import second, and those two columns ARE dictized and returned by c4w_post_show/list to any consumer. Drop the 'ordering matches the legacy site' claim entirely, and note instead that updated_on is currently ordered by nothing and rendered by nothing in c4w — it is carried for fidelity and audit only.
corrections.evidence: ckanext/c4w/logic/action/posts.py spec(): orderings has exactly the keys 'created' and 'title'; get_actions() returns only show and list. query.py:270-272: `order = data_dict.get('order') or spec.default_order; if order not in spec.orderings: order = spec.default_order`. constants.py:412-416 DEFAULT_ORDERINGS = (('modified','Most Recent Updated'),('name','A-Z'),('created','Most Recent Created')). src/blog/views.py:9 `queryset = Post.objects.filter(status=1).order_by('-sticky','-created_on')`.

corrections.problem: The spec's central justification for the lossy plain-text conversion is "is NEVER rendered as HTML: post_card.html does {{ post.excerpt | striptags | truncate(200) }} and no template passes it through | safe". That is true of the c4w templates and FALSE of the source system: all four Django blog list templates render {{ post.excerpt | safe }}. The concrete casualty the spec never names is post id=9, whose excerpt contains a live anchor that Django rendered as a clickable link.
corrections.fix: Correct the sentence to "is never rendered as HTML BY THE C4W TEMPLATES (Django rendered it with | safe)", name post 9's lost hyperlink, and promote extras.excerpt_html from "belt-and-braces" to REQUIRED — it is the only remaining record of that link's href once the excerpt is flattened. Also note the c4w detail page renders no excerpt at all, so Django's og:description / twitter:description meta tags (post_detail.html:16,20) have no target column.
corrections.evidence:
src/themes/citizens4water/templates/blog/blog.html:37 `

{{post.excerpt | safe }}

` (identical at netherlands/blog.html:34, spain/blog.html:34, blog/templates/blog/blog.html:42). SQL: SELECT id,excerpt FROM blog_post WHERE excerpt ~* ' id=9 contains `...can be watched here.` I independently reproduced the spec's false-positive table exactly: color 4/0, style 6/0, font 4/0, span 4/0, rgb 3/0, div 1/0, http 1/0 (raw ILIKE vs regexp_replace-stripped).

corrections.problem: The spec argues a NULL author_id is "harmless for the 14 published Karen posts (no template renders a byline)". True of c4w, false of the legacy site, which rendered a byline on every card and on the detail page. Worse, the byline's display half lives in profiles_profile.surname, a table the spec never lists and never reads, so its extras fallback (legacy_author_name = 'Karen', legacy_author_email) captures only half of what the legacy page showed.
corrections.fix: Reword to "no C4W template renders a byline, so the loss is invisible in the target but IS a fidelity loss against the legacy page." Record legacy_author_name (authtools_user.name), legacy_author_email AND legacy_author_fullname (profiles_profile.surname) for ALL 16 posts unconditionally — not only on a lookup miss — so the byline is restorable whatever the CKAN resolution turns up. Note that for user 8 the surname is the CKAN 'fullname' mirrored by the login backend, so it is authoritative; for user 5 it was hand-entered.
corrections.evidence: src/themes/citizens4water/templates/blog/blog.html:25-29 `{% if post.author.name != "Empty user" %}{{ post.author.name }}{% endif %}{% if post.author.profile.surname %}{{ post.author.profile.surname }},{% endif %}`; src/blog/templates/blog/post_detail.html:39-40 `{% if post.author.surname %}{{ post.author.surname }}{% endif %}`. SQL: SELECT p.user_id,u.name,u.email,p.surname FROM profiles_profile p JOIN authtools_user u ON u.id=p.user_id WHERE p.user_id IN (1,5,8) -> 8|amertens|a.mertens@unesco.org|Annelies Mertens ; 1|Admin|jbarba@ibercivis.es|(empty) ; 5|Karen|karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be|Verstraelen. So the legacy byline on 14 of 16 cards read "Karen Verstraelen". Backend confirmation: themes/citizens4water/backends/ckanlogin.py mirrors CKAN fullname into Profile.surname. (Everything else in this field entry verified sound: 0 FK orphans, 1/14/1 post split, name_match = re.compile('[a-z0-9_\-]*$') at ckan/logic/validators.py:375, 6 users with illegal names, Jef duplicated at ids 10/17, empty password only on id 8.)

corrections.problem: The note says "legacy_id carries no 301 for this entity". Literally true about 301s, but it reads as "the numeric reference does not resolve", and it does. /blog/<slug> is registered with Flask's default STRING converter, and _common.get_by_reference falls back slug -> int(reference) -> legacy_id, so GET /blog/3 returns post 3 with HTTP 200 and no canonicalisation — a second live URL for every post, with no redirect to the slug.
corrections.fix: Say "no 301 is registered, but /blog/<n> still RESOLVES 200 via get_by_reference's legacy_id fallback, giving every post a duplicate uncanonicalised URL." Django never published that shape (its only detail route was the dated one), so there are no inbound links to preserve — which argues for canonicalising it rather than leaving two addresses.
corrections.evidence: blueprint.py:148-152: the `if item_path != list_path:` guard skips the '%s/<int:legacy_id>' rule for post (both paths are '/blog'), then registers `bp.add_url_rule('%s/<slug>' % item_path, detail_endpoint, ...)`. _common.py get_by_reference(): filters on slug, then `legacy_id = int(reference)` and filters on model_cls.legacy_id, then on id. views_catalogue.detail() renders directly with no redirect; only views_catalogue.legacy() issues the 301 and it is never wired for post.

missed_anomalies.what: sanitize_rich_html FAILS CLOSED to a total tag strip when bleach is not importable, destroying every post body corpus-wide with no error. The spec's entire anomaly 1 is measured on the assumption that bleach is present; it never tests the other branch, which is a far bigger silent-corruption path than the img/iframe loss it does report.
missed_anomalies.evidence: sanitize.py::_clean wraps `import bleach` in try/except ImportError and on failure returns `_TAG_RE.sub('', html)` with _TAG_RE = re.compile(r'<[^>]*>'). bleach is declared in setup.py install_requires but imported lazily inside the try, so nothing fails loudly. On this workstation the default interpreter has no bleach: `python3 -c "import bleach"` -> ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'bleach'. I ran the REAL module through that branch over all 16 bodies: total 86057 -> 47920 chars, and anchors `<a` 32 -> 0. For contrast I installed bleach 6.4.0 in a venv and re-ran the same module: 86057 -> 54165 (62.9% retained), reproducing the spec's number exactly, with tag deltas img 17->0, iframe 2->0, h6 9->0, figcaption 13->0, figure 2->0, span 99->0, div 62->0, font 27->0, and a/p/br/h3/li/ol/em/b/i/u/strong/blockquote all unchanged.
missed_anomalies.impact: An importer run in a virtualenv where bleach failed to install writes 16 posts of tagless plain text: every paragraph, heading, list and all 32 outbound links (zenodo, plastic-pirates, unesco, three mailto addresses) gone. The row count is right, the legacy_ids are right, the titles are right, the prose is all still there — so every assertion the spec proposes (16 rows, 15 published, 16 distinct slugs) passes. The 62.9%-vs-55.7% retention difference is invisible without a baseline.
missed_anomalies.handling: Make the importer refuse to start unless `import bleach` succeeds — a hard precondition check before the first INSERT, not a lazy import at first use. Then add a per-post invariant that survives both branches: count `<a` before and after sanitising and abort if the delta is non-zero (32 anchors in, 32 out is true under bleach and catastrophically false without it). Record the bleach version in the import log alongside the retention ratio.

missed_anomalies.what: There is an EIGHTEENTH in-body image in post 3 that the spec's src regex cannot see: a Wix `<image-component>` custom element whose image reference is buried inside an HTML-escaped JSON attribute, with no src= of its own. The spec asserts "All 19 srcs enumerated" and drives the whole media upload from `src="(/citizens4water/media/[^\"]+)"`.
missed_anomalies.evidence: The spec's own census regex `<\s*([a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*)` truncates at the hyphen and reports this as tag `image|1` — a row present in my run of that exact query but absent from the census the spec quotes. Re-run hyphen-aware: SELECT lower(m[1]),count(*) FROM (SELECT regexp_matches(content,'<\s*([a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9-]*)','g') m FROM blog_post) s WHERE m[1] LIKE '%-%' GROUP BY 1 -> image-component|1. The markup (post 3): `
missed_anomalies.impact: The spec's inline-media inventory is 17 of 18 image references. A post-import assertion built on the src regex ("every img in the body has a media_map row") passes while this one is silently absent, and the file is unrecoverable from MEDIA_ROOT because it never lived there. It also already fails to render in Django — browsers ignore an unknown element — so post 3 SHIPS an orphaned photo credit today, before any sanitiser runs. That means the spec's anomaly 3 ("credit lines survive as orphans") is partly a pre-existing legacy defect, not purely a sanitiser artefact, and any "no regression" diff must account for it.
missed_anomalies.handling: Scan content for `data-node-attrs` (1 row: post 3) and for any element name containing a hyphen before the media pass, and record the extracted Wix media id in extras.inline_media with new_url=null and a source='wix-unresolvable' marker, so the inventory is honest at 18 rather than silently 17. Do not attempt to fetch it. Flag post 3 for a human to re-attach or delete the caption, since the caption is real editorial text and the image is not retrievable.

missed_anomalies.what: Four of post 4's seven
missed_anomalies.evidence:
SELECT id, count of ' id=3: figure=2, figcaption=6, img=6 ; id=4: figure=0, figcaption=7, img=3. So post 4 carries 4 more captions than images and zero figure elements — the captions sit bare inside
. Sample caption text recovered from post 4: 'A participating school (De Pagaaier in Nieuwpoort) collecting and quantifying plastic waste at the Yzer river (source: Line Debaveye, VLIZ)'. Post 3's apparent 6/6 balance is also misleading once the image-component above is counted: 6 figcaptions against 6 plus 1 unrenderable image-component inside its own
missed_anomalies.impact: Whichever way the allowlist decision goes, post 4 ends up with 4 credit lines naming photographers for photos that were never in the document. If the img decision is 'restore', an importer that pairs caption-to-preceding-img will mis-pair: with 3 images and 7 captions in document order, at least 4 pairings are wrong, which attributes the wrong photographer to the wrong photo — confidently incorrect output rather than an obvious gap.
missed_anomalies.handling: Do not pair captions to images positionally. Extract each figcaption's text with its document ordinal into extras.inline_media as a separate 'caption' entry keyed on ordinal, and only bind a caption to an image when the caption is a direct sibling/descendant of the same figure (true for post 3's two figures, false for all seven of post 4's). Report the 4 unbindable captions in post 4 for editorial review rather than emitting them next to an arbitrary image.

missed_anomalies.what: constants.py — the file the brief designates as holding "every controlled vocabulary" — contains NO post-status vocabulary, and the key 'status' in COLUMN_VOCABULARIES is bound to the six-value PROJECT vocabulary. The spec proposes {0:'draft', 1:'published'} without ever checking constants.py for it.
missed_anomalies.evidence: constants.py:61-68 STATUSES = (('not-started','Not yet started'),('active','Active'),('periodically-active','Periodically active'),('on-hold','On hold'),('completed','Completed'),('abandoned','Abandoned')); constants.py:293-294 COLUMN_VOCABULARIES = {'status': STATUSES, ...}. grep -in 'draft|publish' constants.py returns only lines 45-46, a prose comment: "``post`` is absent on purpose: a blog post uses a draft/published status set by its author, not a reviewer decision." The literals themselves exist in exactly two places, both hard-coded: query.py:78 `query.filter(model_cls.status == u'published')` and _common.py:59 `published = row.status == u'published'`. Data confirms the source side: SELECT status,count(*) FROM blog_post GROUP BY 1 -> 0|1, 1|15, no CHECK constraint, no third value.
missed_anomalies.impact: The importer's mapping dict has no definition in the contract file, so three independent copies of the string 'published' (importer, query.py, _common.py) must be kept in sync by hand — precisely the drift constants.py exists to prevent, and the spec's own anomaly 4 identifies this literal as "the one place the importer can silently blank the whole news section". Separately, the parameter name 'status' already resolves to project statuses in make_facets (_common.py builds options from constants.COLUMN_VOCABULARIES.get(param)), so the two meanings of 'status' collide by name in a shared lookup.
missed_anomalies.handling: Add POST_STATUSES = (('draft','Draft'), ('published','Published')) to constants.py and have the importer, _public_filter and _common.is_visible all read it — one definition, three consumers. Keep the mapping keyed on the INTEGER exactly as the spec says (the 'Publish'-vs-'published' anomaly is real and correctly diagnosed), and raise on any value outside {0,1}. Do not reuse the key 'status' in COLUMN_VOCABULARIES for posts.

missed_anomalies.what: Post 7's body links to a Django static page that the brief maps to DROP, and the c4w blueprint registers no route for it. The spec's rewrite pass only inspects src attributes and never inventories hrefs, so this dies silently.
missed_anomalies.evidence: Full href enumeration over content: SELECT id,(regexp_matches(content,'href="([^"]+)"','g'))[1] FROM blog_post -> 32 links. Four are absolute self-references to the legacy host: posts 12, 15, 16 point at https://ihp-wins.unesco.org/citizens4water/project/40 | /47 | /30, and post 7 points at https://ihp-wins.unesco.org/citizens4water/p/submit-a-project. The three /project/<n> links SURVIVE, because blueprint.py:111-112 registers `/project/<int:legacy_id>` and views_catalogue.legacy() 301s to the slug. The /p/ one does not: grep -n "'/p/" blueprint.py -> no match, and the brief lists "Django static pages" as out of scope, map to DROP. Also worth noting: bleach strips target="_blank" (32 occurrences of `target=` in content, and 'target' is absent from RICH_ALLOWED_ATTRS), so all 32 surviving external links change to same-tab navigation.
missed_anomalies.impact: One published post ships a dead call-to-action link ("submit a project") pointing at a URL that will 404 on the same domain after cutover — the worst kind of broken link, because the host still answers. It cannot be caught by any media check, since it is an href, not a src, and the spec's rewrite pass never looks at hrefs at all.
missed_anomalies.handling: Inventory hrefs, not just srcs, in the pre-sanitize pass. Classify the four self-referencing absolute URLs: rewrite the three /citizens4water/project/<n> links to relative /citizens4water/project/<n> (they 301 correctly) and escalate the /p/submit-a-project one — either point it at whatever c4w surface replaces the submission page, or flag post 7 for an editorial fix. Add a post-import link check that resolves every self-host href against the registered blueprint rules and fails on a miss.

coverage_gaps: No gaps in blog_post: information_schema.columns returns exactly 14 columns (id, title, title_en, slug, updated_on, content, content_en, excerpt, excerpt_en, image, created_on, sticky, status, author_id) and the spec has a field entry for every one. No gaps in django_summernote_attachment either: all 4 columns (id, name, file, uploaded) are covered.

authtools_user.is_active — the spec declares authtools_user in tables_covered and reads id/name/email/password, but never mentions is_active. It is the column that decides whether an author account is still valid, and the author-resolution pre-flight the spec proposes should check it. No live impact here (all three blog authors are is_active=true), but it is unstated.

authtools_user.is_superuser, is_staff, last_login, date_joined — unmentioned in a table the spec declares covered. is_superuser/is_staff are true for all three blog authors, which is itself notable: every blog author is a Django superuser, so 'author' here means 'site editor', not 'community member'.

profiles_profile.surname — not listed in tables_covered and never read, yet it is the display half of the byline the Django blog rendered on every post card ({{ post.author.profile.surname }}). Values for the three blog authors: 'Verstraelen' (14 posts), 'Annelies Mertens' (1 post), '' (the draft). Dropping user profiles as an entity is in scope per the brief; silently dropping the byline string attached to 15 published posts is a separate decision the spec never surfaces.

blog_post.image's Django default 'default_blog.png' — the spec correctly measures 0/16 rows carrying it, but the media inventory never asks whether MEDIA_ROOT/default_blog.png exists or whether any OTHER entity's importer will need it. Minor, and the spec does say to guard for it.

django_summernote_attachment has no post_id / foreign key of any kind — the spec says this ("NOT a column of blog_post") but does not state the consequence for idempotency: c4w_media_map is keyed on legacy_path with no entity link, so a re-run cannot tell which post an orphaned upload belonged to. The proposed extras.inline_media manifest is the only place that association would live, which makes it load-bearing rather than optional.

anomalies.what: Three usernames that own 36 of the 124 authorship references DO NOT EXIST in CKAN, so created_by / author_id cannot be resolved for them. They are Admin (Django id 1), Karen (id 5) and Liza (id 62).
anomalies.evidence: Ran user_show for all 36 referenced usernames: `curl -s 'https://ihp-wins.unesco.org/api/3/action/user_show?id=<name>'`. 33 returned success=true; `Karen`, `Admin` and `Liza` each returned {"error":{"__type":"Not Found Error"},"success":false}, and so did the lowercase fallbacks `karen`, `admin`, `liza`. Per-table impact, from a JOIN of each entity table to authtools_user WHERE u.name IN ('Admin','Karen','Liza'): blog_post.author_id Karen=14 Admin=1; events_event.creator_id Karen=6 Liza=6; platforms_platform.creator_id Karen=3; projects_project.creator_id Karen=2 Admin=2; resources_resource.creator_id Karen=1; organisations_organisation_editors.user_id Karen=1. Total 36 of the 124 non-NULL authorship rows (SELECT of the eight sources totals 125 rows, 124 non-NULL).
anomalies.impact: A naive importer either crashes on the NotFound from user_show, or silently writes created_by=NULL for 14 of 16 blog posts, 12 of 13 events and 3 of 4 platforms. Because ckanext/c4w/logic/action/_common.py grants visibility of unapproved content via `row.created_by == user.id`, a NULL there makes 4 unapproved projects (ids 6, 7 owned by Admin; 11, 24 owned by Karen) and 1 draft post (id 1, Admin) visible to sysadmins ONLY -- their real owners lose the ability to see or fix their own pending submissions. Attribution on the majority of the blog and the entire events calendar is lost.
anomalies.handling: Fail the import loudly on an unresolvable username rather than defaulting to NULL, and require the operator to supply an explicit alias map (a --user-alias file) before the run proceeds. Seed that map with the one verified candidate: CKAN user `karenverst` exists with fullname 'Karen Verstraelen' (user_show succeeds), which matches profiles_profile.surname='Verstraelen' for Django user 5 -- almost certainly the same human's real CKAN account, but a human must confirm it. No CKAN account was found for Admin or Liza; those two need a product decision (map to ckan_admin, or leave NULL). Independently, always write extras.legacy_created_by_username and extras.legacy_created_by_email so the attribution can be repaired later without re-reading the Django database.

anomalies.what: authtools_user.name has NO unique constraint and is genuinely duplicated: two different people are both called 'Jef'.
anomalies.evidence: `\d authtools_user` shows only two uniqueness guarantees: authtools_user_pkey on id, and authtools_user_email_key UNIQUE (email). There is no index on name. `SELECT name, count(*), string_agg(id::text||':'||email,' | ') FROM authtools_user GROUP BY name HAVING count(*)>1` returns exactly one row: `Jef|2|17:jef@scivil.be | 10:jef.vanlaer.ext@imec.be`. Aggregate check: 62 rows, 61 distinct name, 61 distinct lower(name), 62 distinct email.
anomalies.impact: Any importer that builds a `{name: user_id}` dict from authtools_user, or that resolves in the reverse direction (CKAN username -> Django row) to pick up the email, silently collapses the two Jefs into one -- last writer wins -- and would attribute one person's content to the other. It also breaks the assumption behind ckanlogin.py's own `User.objects.get_or_create(name=...)`, which would now raise MultipleObjectsReturned for that name.
anomalies.handling: Key every internal map on authtools_user.id, never on name. Resolve id -> name -> CKAN id as a per-row lookup, and assert that the map from Django id to CKAN id is a function (it need not be injective). Neither Jef appears as a creator, author or editor of any entity, so this duplicate does not corrupt v1 data -- but the code must not depend on that accident.

anomalies.what: Six usernames are not legal CKAN usernames (leading uppercase), and they are exactly the six accounts that were created outside the CKAN login backend.
anomalies.evidence: `SELECT id,name,email FROM authtools_user WHERE NOT (name ~ '^[a-z0-9_-]{2,100}$')` returns 6 rows: 1 Admin, 2 Jorge, 5 Karen, 10 Jef, 17 Jef, 62 Liza. Every one fails only on has_upper; none has a space or any other illegal character, and all are 3-5 chars long. Independently, `SELECT id,name FROM authtools_user WHERE password LIKE 'pbkdf2%'` returns the SAME six ids -- the other 56 rows have a zero-length password (`SELECT left(password,1), length(password), count(*) ... GROUP BY 1,2` -> `''|0|56` and `p|88|6`). themes/citizens4water/backends/ckanlogin.py creates users with `get_or_create(name=user_info['name'], defaults={'email': ...})` and never sets a password, so an empty password is the signature of a CKAN-originated account.
anomalies.impact: CKAN's name_validator enforces `[a-z0-9_-]*`, so these six names can never exist as CKAN usernames -- the lookup is guaranteed to fail, not merely likely to. An importer that assumes 'the Django name is the CKAN name, so it will resolve' has a 100% failure rate on exactly this set, and no retry, lowercasing or slugification will fix it (the lowercase forms karen/admin/liza/jef were all tested and are all absent from CKAN).
anomalies.handling: Use the regex as a PRE-FLIGHT gate: before touching any entity, validate every distinct referenced name against `^[a-z0-9_-]{2,100}$` and against user_show, and print the reconciliation table (django_id, name, email, resolved CKAN id or MISSING) for the operator to sign off. This turns a 36-row silent data loss into a checklist item resolved before the first INSERT.

anomalies.what: authtools_user.email is a stale creation-time snapshot, and one heavily-used account (ckan_admin) is a shared UNESCO sysadmin login whose Django email belongs to a different person.
anomalies.evidence: For each of the 33 resolvable users I compared md5(lower(strip(django_email))) to the email_hash returned by CKAN user_show (CKAN computes email_hash the same way). Result: 32 match, 1 differs -- Django user 6 `ckan_admin` stores projas@cazalac.org while CKAN's ckan_admin is fullname 'IHP-WINS', sysadmin=true, created 2023-09-29, with 365 packages. ckanlogin.py sets email only inside get_or_create defaults and never updates it on subsequent logins. ckan_admin is the second-heaviest creator in the dataset with 24 authorship references (4 projects, 2 resources, and organisations).
anomalies.impact: Two failure modes. First, an importer that matches Django users to CKAN by EMAIL instead of by name would mis-map or fail to map ckan_admin. Second, and not fixable by code: 24 entities are attributed to a shared sysadmin account rather than to the human who actually submitted them, so `created_by` for those rows grants edit rights to whoever holds the shared credential.
anomalies.handling: Match on name only; treat email purely as provenance (extras.legacy_created_by_email) and as the operator's reconciliation aid. Flag the 24 ckan_admin-owned entities in the pre-flight report as 'shared account -- confirm intended owner' rather than importing them silently. Note that projects 9, 32 and 33, all created by ckan_admin, carry a DIFFERENT human's name and address in projects_project.author/author_email (Annelies Mertens, Mbali Mashele, Zulmira Rodrigues), which is the best available hint at the real submitter.

anomalies.what: events_event.creator_id is the only NULLABLE creator FK, and one row is actually NULL.
anomalies.evidence: `CREATE TABLE public.events_event (... creator_id integer, ...)` -- no NOT NULL, unlike projects_project, organisations_organisation, resources_resource and platforms_platform, which all declare `creator_id integer NOT NULL`. `SELECT count(*) FROM events_event WHERE creator_id IS NULL` returns 1; the row is `6|CS4Water Conference 2025||f||` (also approved=false, mainOrganisation_id NULL, project_id NULL).
anomalies.impact: An importer that writes one shared `resolve_user(row.creator_id)` helper and asserts a non-NULL result -- reasonable, since four of the five entity tables guarantee it -- raises on event 6 and aborts the events pass partway through. If it instead indexes a `{django_id: ckan_id}` dict with the NULL key, it raises KeyError. Either way the whole events import fails on the very last table.
anomalies.handling: Make the resolver accept None and return None, and let c4w_event.created_by be NULL for event 6. Combined with the previous anomaly, this means ZERO of the 13 events get a resolvable owner (6 Karen + 6 Liza + 1 NULL), so the events import must not treat a fully-NULL created_by column as evidence of a bug.

anomalies.what: blog_post.image is the only image column with no directory prefix -- the files live at the MEDIA_ROOT root, not under images/.
anomalies.evidence: blog/models.py:26 is `image = models.ImageField(max_length=200, default='default_blog.png')` with NO upload_to, while every other ImageField declares `upload_to='images/'` (projects/models.py:292,294,296; organisations/models.py:27; platforms/models.py:47,50; resources/models.py:99,101). The data agrees: grouping the 148 distinct entity paths by first path segment gives `images/`=132 and `<no-prefix>`=16, and the 16 unprefixed values are exactly the 16 blog_post.image rows ('5878303.jpg', 'RiverWatch.jpeg', 'Zaniel_April_from_GroundTruth_taking_a_water_sample_from_the_Mthinzima_wetland.JPEG', ...).
anomalies.impact: A media importer that builds its fetch URL as MEDIA_URL + 'images/' + basename -- an easy simplification once you have seen 132 consecutive images/ paths -- 404s on all 16 blog images, which are also the four largest files in the dataset. Conversely, a naive `path.split('/')[1]` to strip the prefix raises IndexError on every blog row.
anomalies.handling: Never synthesise the prefix. Concatenate the stored value verbatim onto the media base: 'https://ihp-wins.unesco.org/citizens4water/media/' + urllib.parse.quote(path). Store the same verbatim value as c4w_media_map.legacy_path so the /citizens4water/media/<path> redirect resolves for both shapes. Verified: all 165 files return HTTP 200 with an image/* content type under that exact construction.

anomalies.what: Six blog posts embed 17 distinct /citizens4water/media/django-summernote/ image URLs inline in their HTML, in BOTH content and content_en. These images are unreachable from any foreign key.
anomalies.evidence: I scanned EVERY text/varchar column of EVERY base table in the database for '/media/|django-summernote' by generating the scan from information_schema.columns. Exactly three columns match: blog_post.content (6 rows), blog_post.content_en (6 rows), and django_summernote_attachment.file (34 rows, the attachment table itself). Nothing else in the database -- not projects_project.description, not any organisation/platform/event/resource body, not pages_pages.content -- contains a media reference. The 6 posts are ids 3, 4, 5, 8, 12, 13. Extracting with regexp_matches(v,'(?:src|href)="([^"]*media[^"]*)"','g') yields 17 distinct URLs, all of the form /citizens4water/media/django-summernote/YYYY-MM-DD/.. Raw HTML sample from post 12: ``.
anomalies.impact: django_summernote_attachment has no FK to blog_post -- the ONLY link is the literal string inside the HTML. An importer that walks foreign keys to build its file list will never see these 17 files, will not upload them, and will not rewrite the URLs. The posts then render with 17 broken images the moment the legacy Django host is decommissioned, and the failure is invisible until someone opens those six posts. This is the single easiest thing to miss in the whole migration.
anomalies.handling: Two-pass. Pass 1: regex blog_post.content for `/citizens4water/media/([^"']+)`, add each captured path to the fetch set alongside the 148 FK-reachable paths, upload, and record c4w_media_map(legacy_path, new_url, sha256). Pass 2: rewrite each occurrence in the body to the new_url before writing c4w_post.content. Import content and DROP content_en (they are byte-identical in all 16 rows), so the rewrite runs once. Also skip the 17 attachments that no body references -- `SELECT a.id, a.file FROM django_summernote_attachment a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT coalesce(content,'')||coalesce(content_en,'') v FROM blog_post) t WHERE t.v LIKE '%'||a.file||'%')` returns ids 1-13, 25, 26, 29, 31, all dead uploads.

anomalies.what: Three projects store an already-RENDERED easy_thumbnails file as their own image1, with the thumbnail suffix baked into the filename.
anomalies.evidence: `SELECT ... WHERE p ~ '\.[0-9]+x[0-9]+_'` over the entity image columns returns 3 rows, all projects_project.image1: #14 `images/2026-02-10_171702023939_851_2025-11-13_080811110404_148_2020-04-07_030304042727_500_Gespot_46_iSPEXlogo.png.600x400_q85_crop.png`, #17 `images/2026-02-10_171702023232_654_2025-11-14_111111114141_748_LW_logo_blue.png.600x400_q85_crop.png`, #30 `images/2026-02-10_171702024747_321_2026-02-09_151502023939_83_Logo.jpg.600x400_q85.jpg`. Note the nested date-stamp prefixes: an admin downloaded a rendered thumbnail and re-uploaded it, twice for #14. All three return HTTP 200 as ordinary files. Separately, 0 of the 148 distinct entity paths appear in easy_thumbnails_thumbnail.name, so these are the only cases and they are stored as originals, not resolved through the thumbnail table.
anomalies.impact: An importer that tries to be clever -- stripping a `.WxH_q85[_crop].ext` suffix to 'recover the original', or skipping paths that look like generated thumbnails to avoid importing derived files -- drops or 404s the main listing image of three projects. The names look like derived artefacts but are the only copy that exists under that path.
anomalies.handling: Treat every entity image value as an opaque path. Never parse, normalise or filter it; fetch exactly what is stored. The correct rule for ignoring derived files is 'do not read easy_thumbnails_* at all', not 'pattern-match filenames'.

anomalies.what: The easy_thumbnails tables are both derived AND stale, and are a trap in both directions: they over-cover by 480 rows and under-cover the live set by 2 files.
anomalies.evidence: easy_thumbnails_source=203 rows, easy_thumbnails_thumbnail=423 rows, easy_thumbnails_thumbnaildimensions=0. Cross-checking source names against the 148 live entity paths: 146 still referenced, 57 ORPHANED (replaced or deleted originals, plus the four repo placeholders void_600.png, void_1100.png, default_blog.png, default_profile.png, and one dead profile_pics/ entry even though profiles_profile.picture is NULL in all 62 rows). In the other direction, 2 live entity paths have NO source row: projects_project #41 image2 `images/2026-03-23_111103031616_322_GT_Logo_Landscape.png` and #41 image3 `images/..._957_Young_Water_Professionals_...JPEG` -- both nonetheless return HTTP 200, they were simply never rendered through a thumbnail tag. Also 0 source rows have a 'django-summernote/' prefix, so inline blog images were served full-size and are absent from this table entirely.
anomalies.impact: Using easy_thumbnails_source as the file inventory -- the obvious move, since it looks like a manifest -- fetches 57 dead files, misses 2 live ones, and misses all 17 inline summernote images. Using easy_thumbnails_thumbnail fetches 423 regenerable derivatives, roughly tripling the transfer for files CKAN will re-render anyway.
anomalies.handling: Ignore all three easy_thumbnails tables completely. Derive the fetch list from exactly two sources: the nine entity image columns (148 paths) and the regex over blog_post.content (17 paths) = 165 files, 35.6 MB, all verified HTTP 200 with an image/* content type.

anomalies.what: 165 files but only 147 distinct contents: 18 pairs of media paths are byte-identical.
anomalies.evidence: I downloaded all 165 files and hashed them. `cut -f1 media_sha.tsv | sort | uniq -c | awk '$1>1'` gives 18 hashes with a count of 2 and none higher; distinct sha256 = 147; total bytes 37,343,744 vs 32,922,990 deduplicated. Two distinct causes. (a) Same file used as image1 AND image2 of the SAME project -- ids 19, 34, 36, 38, 49, e.g. `images/2026-02-11_111102021414_666_THRB_Logo_BlueOnYellow.jpeg` and `..._599_THRB_Logo_BlueOnYellow.jpeg` both sha d6a10f88... (b) DUPLICATE PROJECT SUBMISSIONS -- project pairs 15/16, 21/22, 25/26, 40/41, 43/44 and 31/35 share images across every populated slot, e.g. projects 43 and 44 share all three of image1, image2 and image3 by hash.
anomalies.impact: Not a corruption risk, but 18 redundant uploads, and more importantly a signal the entity-level importers should see: six pairs of projects are near-certain duplicate submissions, which would otherwise surface only as odd-looking twins in the public listing. Naively assuming 'one legacy path = one uploaded file' is also what makes a re-run non-idempotent if new_url is generated per-upload rather than looked up.
anomalies.handling: c4w_media_map already has the right shape: fetch, sha256, and if that sha is already present reuse its new_url while still inserting a NEW row for the second legacy_path. The UNIQUE index is on legacy_path, not on sha256, so many paths mapping to one URL is legal and is what keeps every legacy /citizens4water/media/<path> redirect resolving. Report the six duplicate project pairs to whoever owns the projects mapping.

anomalies.what: Media filenames contain spaces, commas, parentheses, an apostrophe, a tilde and non-ASCII characters, so the path cannot be pasted into a URL unencoded.
anomalies.evidence: Over the 148 distinct entity paths: 11 contain a space, 2 contain a comma, 11 contain a parenthesis, 1 contains an apostrophe, 2 contain a tilde, 2 contain non-ASCII (`p ~ '[^ -~]'`). 0 contain #, +, & or a backslash; 0 are whitespace-only; 0 are untrimmed; 0 have a doubled 'images/images/' prefix. Concrete examples: `images/2026-04-29_121204043434_464_Logo AFR'EAU Fond Blanc.jpg`, `images/2026-02-08_060602022121_545_ChatGPT_Image_Feb_8,_2026,_12_15_12_PM.png`, `images/2025-11-13_151511110505_879_Sin_título.png`, `images/2026-04-17_060604044646_760_Datastream-monogram_blue (1).png`, `images/2025-11-13_151511110505_365_PRE504~1.PNG`. Extensions are mixed case: png=80, jpg=59, jpeg=12, JPEG=7, JPG=5, PNG=2.
anomalies.impact: An unencoded GET on a path with a space produces a malformed request line; the apostrophe and parentheses break naive shell interpolation; the non-ASCII 'título' breaks any latin-1 assumption. The uppercase .JPEG/.JPG/.PNG extensions (14 files) trip extension whitelists and content-type guessers that compare lowercase-only. I verified each of these shapes fetches correctly ONLY when quoted.
anomalies.handling: Always urllib.parse.quote(path) when building the fetch URL, and lowercase the extension only for the content-type decision, never in the stored legacy_path (the redirect must match what Django stored, byte for byte). Sniff the type from the response Content-Type, not from the extension -- all 165 responses carry a correct image/jpeg or image/png.

anomalies.what: created_by, c4w_post.author_id and c4w_relation.object_id for users all hold a CKAN user UUID, not a username string -- the target schema does not say so, and the column type (UnicodeText) does not stop you getting it wrong.
anomalies.evidence: ckanext/c4w/logic/action/_common.py:68 reads `if getattr(row, 'created_by', None) and row.created_by == user.id:` and :70 `if getattr(row, 'author_id', None) and row.author_id == user.id:`; ckanext/c4w/logic/action/projects.py:100 has the same comparison. `user` there is context['auth_user_obj'], a CKAN model.User, whose `.id` is the UUID (user_show for ckan_admin returns id '8ad64841-340c-49dc-8716-c6b61ea4b111', name 'ckan_admin'). The same file resolves the editor relation with `C4wRelation.object_id == user.id`. db.py's own docstring confirms it for relations: "With object_type='user' the object_id is a CKAN user.id".
anomalies.impact: Writing the username into created_by type-checks, imports cleanly, and produces rows that look right in ad-hoc SQL -- and then every ownership check silently returns False. Authors cannot see or edit their own unapproved submissions, and the moderation queue appears to have no owners. Nothing fails loudly; a UnicodeText column accepts either value.
anomalies.handling: The resolver must return user_show(name)['id'] (the UUID), and the importer should assert the returned value matches a UUID shape before writing it, so a future refactor that returns the name fails at import time rather than at page-render time. Keep the human-readable username in extras.legacy_created_by_username for debugging.

anomalies.what: Four blog posts embed absolute links to the legacy host, three of them to numeric legacy project IDs.
anomalies.evidence: Scanning all text columns for 'ihp-wins\.unesco\.org/citizens4water|href="/citizens4water' matches blog_post.content (4 rows), blog_post.content_en (4 rows), pages_pages.content/content_en (7 rows each, out of scope) and core_code_footer.link_url1..6 (1 row each). Extracting from blog bodies: post 12 -> https://ihp-wins.unesco.org/citizens4water/project/40, post 15 -> /project/47, post 16 -> /project/30, post 7 -> /citizens4water/p/submit-a-project. All three project IDs exist (`SELECT id FROM projects_project WHERE id IN (30,40,47)` returns all three; projects_project spans ids 6..49, 43 rows).
anomalies.impact: These are not media, so the media rewrite will not touch them. The three /project/<int> links survive only if the legacy_id -> slug 301 that c4w_project.legacy_id exists for is actually implemented and mounted at the old path; otherwise three blog posts link into a 404. The fourth, /p/submit-a-project, points at a pages_pages row that is explicitly out of scope for v1 and will 404 with no redirect to catch it.
anomalies.handling: Leave the project links alone and let the legacy_id redirect handle them, but add them to the post-migration link-check list so the redirect is verified end-to-end rather than assumed. Raise /p/submit-a-project with product: either keep a minimal static page at that path or rewrite that one link during import.

anomalies.what: projects_project.author / author_email are free-text contact fields that only partly correspond to real users, and several rows hold a URL or an email in the wrong field.
anomalies.evidence: 43 rows: author has 12 empty strings, author_email 11. Only 18 of 43 author_email values match an authtools_user.email exactly, 19 case-insensitively. Joining each project to its creator shows the two are frequently different people: project 9 author 'Annelies Mertens' but creator ckan_admin; project 39 author 'John Wilkinson' (john.wilkinson@york.ac.uk) but creator harrietsleight; project 46 author 'Roland Bischof' (info@flow-projekt.de) but creator plueskow. Projects 21 and 22 store `https://www.parmasostenibile.it/#freshwaterwatch ` in the AUTHOR field; project 38 stores `Info@homeriverbioblitz.org` in the author field. Trailing spaces appear in both columns ('Afnan Agramont ', 'Charlene Russell ', 'fwwparma@parmasostenibile.it ', 'charlene@groundtruth.co.za ').
anomalies.impact: An importer that reads 'author' as authorship and tries to resolve it to a CKAN user, or that folds it into the c4w 'author' free vocabulary alongside authors_author, invents 24 phantom author identities and mis-attributes ownership. Untrimmed values also produce inconsistent display and would slug differently if ever normalised.
anomalies.handling: Copy both to the native c4w_project.author / author_email columns verbatim apart from btrim(), and map the empty string to NULL so 'absent' has one representation. Never resolve them against authtools_user and never feed them to the 'author' term vocabulary -- that vocabulary belongs to authors_author, which serves the resource library only.

anomalies.what: authors_author contains obvious test data and unused rows that must not be imported.
anomalies.evidence: `SELECT a.id, a.author FROM authors_author a ORDER BY a.id` returns 14 rows starting with `1|Lorem ipsum`. resources_resource_authors has only 11 rows; joining them shows author ids 1 ('Lorem ipsum'), 13 ('Meritxell Turó') and 14 ('Anna Witter') are linked to no resource, and resources 1, 4 and 7 have no authors at all. Distribution: resource 2 -> 5 authors, resource 3 -> 3, resource 5 -> 2, resource 6 -> 1.
anomalies.impact: Importing authors_author as a standalone vocabulary rather than through the join table publishes a facet containing 'Lorem ipsum' on the public resource library. Two legitimate-looking names would also appear as facet values matching zero resources.
anomalies.handling: Drive the 'author' term_link rows from resources_resource_authors, not from authors_author. Rows with no join are simply never created. Also note these are bibliographic names, never CKAN users, even where they coincide with one ('Koen Verbist' -> user kverbist, 'Annelies Mertens' -> user amertens) -- they must stay in c4w_term_link, not become c4w_relation user links.

anomalies.what: Three quarters of the editor rows duplicate the entity's own creator, so the editor relation looks redundant but is not.
anomalies.evidence: `SELECT e.project_id, u.name, (u.id = p.creator_id) FROM projects_project_editors e JOIN ... ` gives 4 rows, of which 3 are the creator (projects 23/mreyniers, 28/ingar, 40/ljbutler123 true; project 12/linnaea_cahill false). The org version gives 8 rows, of which 3 are the creator (orgs 12/ingar and 33/ljbutler123 true; orgs 14 x2, 16, 18, 31 x2 false). Total 12 editor rows, 6 distinct 'real' delegations.
anomalies.impact: An importer that de-duplicates 'editor equals creator' as noise drops 6 of 12 c4w_relation rows. Conversely, one that assumes the editors list is disjoint from the creator will double-count contributors on any 'who can edit this' display.
anomalies.handling: Import all 12 rows verbatim as c4w_relation(predicate='editor', object_type='user'). _common.py checks created_by and the editor relation as independent conditions, so a redundant row is harmless and a dropped one removes real access. One caveat: org 31's editor 'Karen' is unresolvable, so that relation row cannot be written -- it falls under the alias-map decision above. Note also there is no resources_resource_editors table at all, so resources have no editor concept to migrate.

anomalies.what: The 'absent' value for image and credit columns is inconsistently the empty string or NULL, and differs per table.
anomalies.evidence: Per-column counts of NULL vs empty string across the nine image columns: every image column has 0 NULLs and uses '' for absent (projects image1 5 empty, image2 14, image3 19; organisations logo 1; platforms profileImage 3; resources image1 1, image2 5), while blog_post.image is NOT NULL and never blank. The credit columns are mixed: projects_project."imageCredit1" has 2 NULL + 39 '', "imageCredit2" 2 NULL + 38 '', "imageCredit3" 1 NULL + 39 ''; resources_resource."imageCredit2" has 1 NULL + 5 ''; but organisations_organisation."logoCredit" and both platform credit columns use '' exclusively. 0 rows anywhere carry a credit without a corresponding image.
anomalies.impact: `if row.image1:` happens to work for both, but `if row.image1 is not None:` treats 5 empty projects as having an image and produces a fetch of MEDIA_URL + '' -- a request for the media directory index. On the credit side, a plain copy leaves c4w with two distinct spellings of 'no credit', so templates need `{% if credit and credit.strip() %}` forever and any COUNT(column) is wrong.
anomalies.handling: Normalise once at the mapping boundary: `value = (raw or '').strip() or None` for every image path and every credit, and only enqueue a fetch when the result is truthy. That yields exactly the measured 148 entity paths.

open_questions: Should Django user 5 'Karen' (27 authorship references, the single largest creator: 14 of 16 blog posts, 3 of 4 platforms, 6 events, 2 projects, 1 resource, 1 org-editor row) be remapped to CKAN user 'karenverst'? Evidence for: user_show('karenverst') returns fullname 'Karen Verstraelen', and profiles_profile.surname for Django user 5 is 'Verstraelen'. Evidence against: different email domains (karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be vs the karenverst account, whose email I cannot read anonymously), and Django user 28 'karenverst' already exists as a SEPARATE row that authored nothing. This needs a human yes/no; it decides the attribution of most of the blog and most of the platforms.

What should own the content of Django users 1 'Admin' (3 refs: 2 unapproved projects, 1 draft post) and 62 'Liza' (6 refs: 6 approved events)? No CKAN account exists under those names or their lowercase forms. Options: leave created_by NULL (content becomes sysadmin-only for the unapproved rows), or attribute to ckan_admin. Note Liza's 6 events are all approved and public, so only attribution is at stake there; Admin's 2 projects and 1 post are unapproved/draft and would become invisible to any non-sysadmin.

Should the 24 entities created under the shared 'ckan_admin' sysadmin account be re-attributed? For 3 of them (projects 9, 32, 33) projects_project.author/author_email name a different real person (Annelies Mertens / a.mertens@unesco.org, Mbali Mashele / m.mashele@unesco.org, Zulmira Rodrigues / z.rodrigues@unesco.org), and amertens is a resolvable CKAN user. Leaving them on ckan_admin grants edit rights to whoever holds the shared credential.

Does the /citizens4water/media/<path> redirect backed by c4w_media_map get implemented in v1? Nothing in ckanext/c4w/blueprint.py currently registers such a route, and c4w_media_map's own docstring says it exists partly to serve it. Without it the 148 legacy image URLs that exist in the wild (search engines, the three blog posts linking to /citizens4water/project/<int>, any external embed) break at cutover even though every file has been re-uploaded.

Is the legacy_id -> slug 301 for /project/<int> actually mounted at the old path prefix, or only inside the new extension's routes? Blog posts 12, 15 and 16 contain absolute links to https://ihp-wins.unesco.org/citizens4water/project/40, /47 and /30 that the media rewrite will not touch and that only that redirect can save.

Blog post 7 links to https://ihp-wins.unesco.org/citizens4water/p/submit-a-project, a pages_pages row that is explicitly out of scope for v1. Keep a stub at that path, rewrite the link during import, or accept the 404?

Should the 17 unreferenced django_summernote_attachment files (ids 1-13, 25, 26, 29, 31) and the 57 orphaned easy_thumbnails_source originals be archived anywhere before the Django host is decommissioned, or is deleting them with the old server acceptable? They are unreachable from any live row, but two of the summernote orphans (29, 31) are full-resolution GroundTruth field photographs whose only other copies are the near-identical ones that ARE referenced.

profiles_profile."contentVisible" is false for 2 users (ids 8 amertens, 10 Jef). I verified it does not gate entity visibility in the current extension code, only the out-of-scope profile page. Confirm with product that hiding a user's contribution list is genuinely not required in v1 -- amertens created 2 entities and authored 1 blog post that would remain publicly attributed to them.

verdict.area: Users, authorship and media (cross-cutting: identity + files)

corrections.problem: Spec states nullable_in_practice = '62 of 62 NULL -- zero non-empty values' and claims it MEASURED 'SELECT DISTINCT coalesce(picture,'<NULL>')' returning the NULL marker. The polarity is inverted: there are ZERO NULLs. All 62 rows hold the EMPTY STRING. The conclusion (no profile pictures to fetch) is right, but the stated fact is wrong, and the spec's own anomaly #17 makes exactly this distinction load-bearing ('if row.image1 is not None: ... produces a fetch of MEDIA_URL + \'\' -- a request for the media directory index'). A reader who trusts the NULL claim and writes `WHERE picture IS NOT NULL` gets 62 spurious fetches of the media root.
corrections.fix: State: '62 of 62 are the empty string; 0 NULL; 0 non-empty.' Apply the same `value = (raw or '').strip() or None` normalisation the spec mandates for the nine image columns, and never branch on `IS NOT NULL` for any Django FileField/CharField in this schema.
corrections.evidence: kubectl --context=default -n ckan exec c4w-postgres-0 -- psql -U citizens4water -d c4w_import -tAc "SELECT quote_literal(coalesce(picture,'<NULL>'))||' x'||count(*) FROM profiles_profile GROUP BY picture;"  ->  '' x62   (single group, the empty string, not the NULL marker). Confirmed by aggregate: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE picture IS NULL) AS picture_null, count(*) FILTER (WHERE coalesce(picture,'')<>'') AS picture_nonempty FROM profiles_profile;  ->  picture_null=0 picture_nonempty=0

corrections.problem: The spec twice asserts that 'resources 1, 4 and 7 have no authors' (once in the resources_resource_authors field row, once in the authors_author anomaly). There is no resource with id 1 — resources_resource holds ids 2,3,4,5,6,7. Only TWO of the six resources lack authors, not three. This is a wrong row-level measurement in the one area where the spec asks the importer to drive term_link creation off the join table, and it implies the author checked ids by assumption rather than by query.
corrections.fix: Replace with: 'resources_resource holds ids 2,3,4,5,6,7 (no id 1). Resources 4 and 7 have no authors; 2->5, 3->3, 5->2, 6->1 = 11 join rows.' Never iterate a legacy id range; always drive from the actual id set.
corrections.evidence: SELECT string_agg(id::text,',' ORDER BY id) FROM resources_resource;  ->  2,3,4,5,6,7  (6 rows, minimum id 2).  SELECT count(*) FROM resources_resource r WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM resources_resource_authors ra WHERE ra.resource_id=r.id);  ->  2. Per-resource distribution from the join: res 2 -> 5 authors (join ids 3-7), res 3 -> 3 (ids 8,9,10), res 5 -> 2 (ids 11,12), res 6 -> 1 (id 13).

corrections.problem: Spec's editor anomaly says 'The org version gives 8 rows, of which 3 are the creator (orgs 12/ingar and 33/ljbutler123 true; orgs 14 x2, 16, 18, 31 x2 false)' — the sentence contradicts itself (claims 3, lists 2, and the 'false' list already accounts for 6 of 8). The field row repeats it as '3 of 8 are also the org's creator (orgs 12, 33)'. Actual overlap is 2. The derived total is therefore also wrong: the spec concludes 'Total 12 editor rows, 6 distinct real delegations' when it is 5 creator-duplicates and 7 genuine delegations.
corrections.fix: Correct to: '12 editor rows total = 5 that duplicate the entity's own creator (projects 23/mreyniers, 28/ingar, 40/ljbutler123; orgs 12/ingar, 33/ljbutler123) + 7 genuine delegations.' The handling advice (import all 12 verbatim; _common.py checks created_by and the editor relation independently) is correct and unaffected.
corrections.evidence: SELECT 'org_editor id='||e.id||' org='||e.organisation_id||' user='||u.name||' is_creator='||(u.id=o.creator_id)::text FROM organisations_organisation_editors e JOIN authtools_user u ON u.id=e.user_id JOIN organisations_organisation o ON o.id=e.organisation_id ORDER BY e.id;  ->  id3 org12 ingar TRUE; id4 org14 crowdwater false; id5 org14 linnaea_cahill false; id6 org16 ajcanepa false; id8 org18 flaviatauro false; id9 org31 anneliesduerinckx false; id10 org31 Karen false; id11 org33 ljbutler123 TRUE.  => 2 true / 6 false. Project side: id5 proj12 linnaea_cahill false; id6 proj23 mreyniers TRUE; id7 proj28 ingar TRUE; id8 proj40 ljbutler123 TRUE => 3 true / 1 false.

corrections.problem: Spec says 'ckan_admin is the second-heaviest creator in the dataset with 24 authorship references (4 projects, 2 resources, and organisations)'. The total 24 is right; the breakdown is not — it is 5 projects and 17 organisations. The spec then asks the operator to 'Flag the 24 ckan_admin-owned entities in the pre-flight report', so the per-table numbers are the ones a human will reconcile against.
corrections.fix: Correct to: 'ckan_admin (Django id 6) holds 24 references: 5 projects, 17 organisations, 2 resources, 0 platforms, 0 events, 0 posts, 0 editor rows.'
corrections.evidence: SELECT 'projects='||(SELECT count(*) FROM projects_project WHERE creator_id=6)||' orgs='||(SELECT count(*) FROM organisations_organisation WHERE creator_id=6)||' resources='||(SELECT count(*) FROM resources_resource WHERE creator_id=6)||' platforms='||(SELECT count(*) FROM platforms_platform WHERE creator_id=6)||' events='||(SELECT count(*) FROM events_event WHERE creator_id=6)||' posts='||(SELECT count(*) FROM blog_post WHERE author_id=6)||' editors='||((SELECT count(*) FROM projects_project_editors WHERE user_id=6)+(SELECT count(*) FROM organisations_organisation_editors WHERE user_id=6));  ->  projects=5 orgs=17 resources=2 platforms=0 events=0 posts=0 editors=0   (5+17+2 = 24)

corrections.problem: The anomaly is scoped explicitly to 'the 148 distinct entity paths' and every other statistic in that bullet is a 148-set number (space=11, comma=2, paren=11, apos=1, tilde=2, non-ASCII=2 — all independently confirmed). But the appended extension histogram 'png=80, jpg=59, jpeg=12, JPEG=7, JPG=5, PNG=2' sums to 165, i.e. it is the entity+inline set. The follow-on claim 'The uppercase .JPEG/.JPG/.PNG extensions (14 files) trip extension whitelists' therefore also mixes scopes; over the 148 entity paths it is 12.
corrections.fix: Split the two scopes: 'Over the 148 entity paths: png=67, jpg=57, jpeg=12, JPEG=5, JPG=5, PNG=2; 12 uppercase. Over all 165 fetched files (entity + inline): png=80, jpg=59, jpeg=12, JPEG=7, JPG=5, PNG=2; 14 uppercase.' The handling (sniff Content-Type, never lowercase the stored legacy_path) is correct.
corrections.evidence: Over the 148 distinct non-blank entity image values: SELECT regexp_replace(p,'^.*\.','') e, count(*) FROM ip GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;  ->  png x67, jpg x57, jpeg x12, JPEG x5, JPG x5, PNG x2  (sum 148). Charset over the same set confirmed exactly as the spec states: space=11 comma=2 paren=11 apos=1 tilde=2 nonascii=2 hash=0 plus=0 amp=0 thumbpat=3 TOTAL=148.

corrections.problem: The spec routes the Django account email into `extras` and instructs it be 'denormalised onto each entity row that user created'. `extras` is not private storage: db.py's entity_dictize merges it at the TOP LEVEL of the dict returned by c4w_*_show / c4w_*_list, and those actions are anonymous-readable. So this publishes 36 individuals' work email addresses (karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be, jef@scivil.be, a.mertens@unesco.org, lm.plueskow@idiv.de, ...) on 125 public entity records and in every anonymous API response. Django never exposed authtools_user.email publicly — it lived only behind /admin. The spec's own stated purpose for the field is 'the operator's reconciliation aid', which is a one-off import concern, not a per-row public attribute. This also violates the stated design rule that a field earns a place in the payload only if the site needs it: nothing filters, facets or renders a creator email.
corrections.fix: Drop legacy_created_by_email from extras entirely. Emit the (django_id, name, email, resolved CKAN id or MISSING) reconciliation table to the pre-flight report FILE the spec already proposes, which the operator reads once and does not publish. Keep extras.legacy_created_by_username — a CKAN username is already public — and note that it is what lets an operator repair attribution later.
