missed_anomalies.what: projects_project.hidden is NULL in 42 of 43 rows, not false. The spec reasons at length about _common.py's visibility logic (approved/hidden/status + created_by/author_id/editor) and builds its largest impact claim on it, but its nullable_in_practice methodology only ever measured text and FK columns — it never checked a boolean on any entity table it touched.
missed_anomalies.evidence: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE approved IS NULL) AS approved_null, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hidden IS NULL) AS hidden_null, count(*) FILTER (WHERE moderated IS NULL) AS moderated_null, count(*) FROM projects_project; -> approved_null=0 hidden_null=42 moderated_null=0 n=43. Visible directly in the unapproved set: SELECT 'proj '||id||' approved='||coalesce(approved::text,'<NULL>')||' hidden='||coalesce(hidden::text,'<NULL>')||' creator_id='||creator_id FROM projects_project WHERE approved IS NOT TRUE OR hidden IS TRUE ORDER BY id; -> proj 6 approved=false hidden=<NULL> creator_id=1; proj 7 ... creator_id=1; proj 11 ... creator_id=5; proj 16 ... creator_id=21; proj 21 ... creator_id=26; proj 24 ... creator_id=5; proj 25 ... creator_id=30; proj 41 ... creator_id=41; proj 44 ... creator_id=42. (This is also why a naive `'proj '||id||' hidden='||p.hidden` probe returns four BLANK LINES instead of four rows — string concatenation with NULL yields NULL, which is how I found it.)
missed_anomalies.impact: Not currently fatal, and I confirmed why: logic/query.py::_public_filter uses `query.filter(model_cls.hidden.isnot(True))`, which is NULL-safe, and _common.py::is_visible uses `if hasattr(row,'hidden') and row.hidden:`, where NULL is falsy in Python. So today a copied NULL behaves like false. The real exposure is future and silent: c4w_project declares Column('hidden', types.Boolean, default=False), so anyone who later writes the more obvious `hidden == False`, or reads COUNT(hidden), or relies on ix_c4w_project_public_modified over (approved, hidden, modified), gets wrong answers for 42 of 43 projects. It also means any audit that spot-checks a project row by string-concatenating its booleans silently returns nothing, which is a trap for the pre-flight report the spec proposes.
missed_anomalies.handling: Normalise on import: `hidden = bool(row.hidden)` (and the same for every Boolean the mapping touches), so the c4w column matches its declared default and no downstream predicate has to be NULL-aware. Add a boolean-nullability sweep to the spec's measurement methodology — the spec measured NULL vs empty-string exhaustively for text, and should do the same for booleans. Confirmed unaffected but worth stating: the spec's claim that projects 6, 7 (Admin) and 11, 24 (Karen) are the unapproved projects owned by unresolvable users is correct.

missed_anomalies.what: The spec's biggest open question — whether Django user 5 'Karen' should be remapped to CKAN user 'karenverst' — is answerable from data the spec already had, and the answer weakens its own recommendation. CKAN publishes email_hash = md5(lower(strip(email))) anonymously; the spec used exactly this technique to check its other 33 users but declared it unavailable here ('different email domains ... vs the karenverst account, whose email I cannot read anonymously').
missed_anomalies.evidence: user_show('karenverst') returns email_hash = ddc3a874f40af50687a7da86f7bcd4b1, fullname 'Karen Verstraelen', id c3250093-47d5-4334-9fa1-e0bbab6dc59c, sysadmin=false, state=active, number_created_packages=0, last_active=null. Computing the hash locally: md5('verstraelenkaren@hotmail.com') = ddc3a874f40af50687a7da86f7bcd4b1 -> EXACT MATCH. md5('karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be') = 5ebdc0d3271a7ac8df3ae0e8511601f5 -> NO match. And SELECT id||'|'||name||'|'||email FROM authtools_user WHERE name ILIKE 'karen%' OR name ILIKE '%verst%'; -> 28|karenverst|verstraelenkaren@hotmail.com AND 5|Karen|karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be. So CKAN 'karenverst' is provably the same account as Django user 28 (which the spec itself notes 'authored nothing'), and is provably NOT Django user 5.
missed_anomalies.impact: This decides the attribution of 27 references — 14 of 16 blog posts, 3 of 4 platforms, 6 events, 2 projects, 1 resource, 1 org-editor row — the single largest block in the migration. The spec presents 'almost certainly the same human's real CKAN account' on the strength of a fullname/surname coincidence alone. The hash evidence keeps the human-identity hypothesis alive (one person, a work imec account used for Django admin and a personal hotmail account registered in CKAN) but shows the two accounts are distinct records with distinct addresses, and that the CKAN target has never been used (0 packages, last_active null). Remapping would attribute 27 production entities, including most of the blog, to an account whose registered contact address is a personal mailbox and whose owner has never logged into it. That is a materially different proposition from what the open question describes, and it is the kind of thing a human sign-off should be shown rather than have to rediscover.
missed_anomalies.handling: Put the hash evidence in the open question so the human decides on facts: 'CKAN karenverst (c3250093-...) is provably Django user 28, not Django user 5. Django user 5 Karen (karen.verstraelen.ext@imec.be) has no CKAN account under any casing. Remapping 5 -> karenverst asserts these are the same person; karenverst has 0 packages and has never been active.' Apply the same anonymous email_hash probe to any future alias-map candidate — it is cheap, it is what the spec already does for the resolvable set, and it converts a guess into a check. Also worth recording as verified-clean: no two of the 33 resolvable Django users map to the same CKAN uuid, so the django_id -> ckan_id map is injective as well as a function.
